laws.title: Dual Currency System & Prohibited Transactions
laws.subtitle: MLC system — US card restrictions for tourists
laws.fullDescription: Cuba operates an MLC (Moneda Libremente Convertible) card-based system for tourists. US credit/debit cards do NOT work in Cuba due to the US embargo. Visitors must bring sufficient cash (euros, Canadian dollars, or other non-US currencies are recommended). Exchanging money at official CADECA offices is required.
laws.penalty: Illegal currency exchange or commerce: criminal penalties under Cuban commercial law.
exceptions: Official CADECA exchange houses are legal
MLC cards issued by non-US banks work normally

quiz.q: Why don't US credit cards work in Cuba?
options: The US trade embargo prevents US card transactions in Cuba
Cuban law bans all foreign cards
quiz.explanation: The US trade embargo prevents US-issued credit and debit cards from working in Cuba.

laws.title: Photography Restrictions — Military and Police
laws.subtitle: Cuban law — Photographing police or military is illegal
laws.fullDescription: In Cuba, photographing police officers, military personnel, military installations, and government buildings is illegal. Tourists have had cameras confiscated and been detained for photographing what appeared to be ordinary scenes that included police or officials. The Cuban government is also sensitive about photography of poverty or material shortages that could be used for negative media coverage.
laws.penalty: Confiscation of camera/equipment. Detention for questioning. In serious cases, deportation or criminal charges.
exceptions: Tourist sites and street scenes without officials
Official government-authorised photography
Journalism with press credentials (very restricted)

quiz.q: What is illegal to photograph in Cuba?
options: Police officers, military personnel, and government buildings
quiz.explanation: Photographing police, military, or government buildings in Cuba is illegal — tourists have been detained and had equipment confiscated for doing so.

laws.title: Cuban Culture — Music, Santería and Warmth
laws.subtitle: Son, salsa and Afro-Cuban religion shape daily life
laws.fullDescription: Cuba is one of the world's most musically rich cultures — son, salsa, jazz, and bolero are everywhere. Greetings are warm: hugs and cheek kisses among friends. Santería (Afro-Cuban religious tradition) is widely practiced — respect ceremonies and don't photograph rituals without permission. Cubans are proud of their culture, history, and revolution. Don't speak negatively of the revolution in public.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty for most cultural missteps — but public criticism of the government or revolution can attract attention from authorities.
exceptions: Private conversations with trusted friends more candid
Tourism industry workers more accustomed to varied perspectives

quiz.q: What is Santería in Cuban culture?
options: An Afro-Cuban religious tradition blending Yoruba and Catholic elements
quiz.explanation: Santería is an Afro-Cuban religion blending Yoruba traditions (brought by enslaved Africans) with Catholic elements — widely practiced and deeply respected in Cuban culture.

laws.title: Internet Censorship — Expensive and Restricted Access
laws.subtitle: ETECSA monopoly — Social media monitored; VPN use risky
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has one of the lowest internet penetration rates and most controlled internet environments in the world. ETECSA is the state telecom monopoly — the only internet provider. Mobile data is expensive. Social media platforms (including WhatsApp, which requires special configuration) are accessible but monitored. VPN use is technically illegal. During protests, internet has been shut down. Anti-government speech online can result in criminal prosecution.
laws.penalty: Anti-government online content: criminal prosecution under Penal Code. VPN use: administratively illegal, selectively enforced.
exceptions: Tourist hotels may have more reliable (but monitored) Wi-Fi
Businesses with ETECSA corporate accounts

quiz.q: Who is the only internet provider in Cuba?
quiz.explanation: ETECSA is Cuba's state monopoly telecom provider — the only legal internet service. Access is expensive, monitored, and occasionally blocked during civil unrest.

laws.title: Cuban Rum — Legal and Celebrated; Import Allowances
laws.subtitle: Cuba's rum (ron) culture — Legal to bring home within limits
laws.fullDescription: Cuba is the world's most famous rum-producing country — Ron Havana Club and dozens of other brands. Rum is central to Cuban culture: mojitos, daiquiris, and Cuba Libres are national drinks. Cuba allows tourists to export up to 3 bottles of rum duty-free (within the international duty-free allowance). US tourists historically faced restrictions on bringing Cuban rum back to the US (due to the embargo) — though small personal quantities were briefly permitted. Mojitos in Havana's La Bodeguita del Medio are a tourist rite of passage.
laws.penalty: No penalty for legal consumption of rum. Exporting more than allowed quantities: customs seizure.
exceptions: Personal quantities for non-US travellers: duty-free limits of home country apply
US embargo has complex rules for US citizens returning with Cuban goods

quiz.q: What is Cuba's most famous rum brand, also central to the US embargo controversy?
quiz.explanation: Havana Club is Cuba's most famous rum brand — subject to trademark battles between the Cuban state and Bacardi (a Cuban exile brand) due to the US embargo and the history of nationalisation.

laws.title: Photography Laws — Military, Officials and Private Property
laws.subtitle: Decree 217 — Photographing military or officials is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Cuba prohibits photography of military installations, police, courts, prisons, airports, ports, and government buildings without authorisation. Decree 217 and the Constitution broadly restrict activities deemed 'against the Revolution.' Foreign journalists must be accredited by the International Press Centre (CPI). Photographing Cuban citizens in ways that could embarrass the state (e.g. poverty, decay) has caused issues for foreign photographers. During the July 2021 protests, social media was blocked and people were arrested for posting images of protests.
laws.penalty: Photographing prohibited locations: confiscation of equipment + arrest + up to 3 years imprisonment. Publishing images critical of government abroad: potential charges on return.
exceptions: Tourist photography of Havana's famous old city and tourist areas is generally fine
Accredited press with CPI credentials
laws.sourceLabel: Cuba Media Law — Decree 217 and Constitution

quiz.q: What happened to Cuba's internet during the July 2021 protests?
options: The government blocked social media and arrested people for posting protest images
Access was slowed but not blocked
quiz.explanation: During Cuba's historic July 2021 protests, the government blocked social media platforms and arrested people for posting images of demonstrations — part of broad restrictions on photography and online expression critical of the Revolution.

laws.title: Cuban Internet and Media Laws — VPNs, Foreign Press and Online Speech Restricted
laws.subtitle: Decree 349/2018 & Penal Code — Criticising the government online can mean prison
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has some of the world's most restricted internet access. Since 2019, mobile internet is available but heavily filtered — social media sites are sometimes blocked. Decree 349 (2018) criminalises unapproved artistic and cultural content. The 2022 Penal Code includes articles criminalising 'dissemination of false information against international peace' and 'enemy propaganda' — used against journalists and activists. Foreign journalists must be accredited through the UPEC (Union of Cuban Journalists) before working. Photographing military installations, police operations, or poverty is sensitive. The US embargo means US visitors have restrictions on purchasing local goods and spending.
laws.penalty: 'Enemy propaganda': up to 8 years. Unauthorized foreign media work: deportation + equipment confiscation. VPN use is not explicitly banned but accessing blocked sites carries risk.
exceptions: Accredited foreign press with UPEC credentials
Academic researchers with approved institutional partnerships
laws.sourceLabel: Human Rights Watch — Cuba Country Report 2024

quiz.q: What Cuban law enacted in 2018 criminalises unapproved artistic and cultural content?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Decreto 349 (2018) criminalises any artistic performance or cultural activity deemed 'contrary to Cuban law or the values of Cuban culture' without government authorisation.

laws.title: Cuban Music and Cultural Exports — ICAP Rules for Artists; Santería Practices
laws.subtitle: ICAP and UNEAC — Cultural performances need permits; Afro-Cuban religion laws
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Institute of Friendship with the Peoples (ICAP) and the National Union of Writers and Artists (UNEAC) regulate all cultural collaborations with foreign visitors. Musicians, dancers, and artists cannot simply perform jointly with foreign visitors without institutional approval — joint recordings or performances for commercial use require contracts through UNEAC. Cuba's Afro-Cuban religions (Santería, Palo Monte, Abakuá) are widely practised and involve ceremonies that outsiders may be invited to observe but must approach respectfully. Photographing Santería ceremonies requires explicit permission from the practitioners. Animal sacrifice during religious ceremonies is legally permitted under Cuban law as a religious freedom right.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised commercial recording with Cuban artists: confiscation + UNEAC complaint. Disrespecting Santería ceremonies: social sanction; possible police involvement if disturbance caused.
exceptions: ICAP-organised cultural exchange programmes
Documented artistic collaborations through UNEAC-approved contracts
laws.sourceLabel: Cuba Government — Cultural Affairs and UNEAC

quiz.q: What is the name of Cuba's National Union of Writers and Artists that must approve commercial cultural collaborations with foreigners?
quiz.explanation: UNEAC (Unión de Escritores y Artistas de Cuba — National Union of Writers and Artists) must approve any commercial cultural collaboration between Cuban artists and foreign visitors — reflecting the state's oversight of cultural production.

laws.title: Internet Access Restrictions — VPN Use and Social Media Controls
laws.subtitle: Cuba heavily restricts internet access; unauthorized VPNs risk legal penalties
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has one of the world's most restricted internet environments, with ETECSA holding a state monopoly on telecommunications. Mobile internet was only introduced in December 2018. Websites critical of the government are routinely blocked, including many international news sites. VPN use is technically illegal under Decree 370 of 2019, which prohibits 'content contrary to social interest, ethics, and public morals.' During the July 2021 protests, internet was shut down entirely. Social media posts deemed critical of the government can result in prosecution under cybercrime laws. Foreign visitors using local SIM cards should be aware that online activity may be monitored.
laws.penalty: Publishing 'harmful content' online: 1–3 years imprisonment. Repeated violations: up to 5 years. VPN use for circumventing state controls: fines up to 3,000 pesos.
exceptions: Diplomatic communications through embassy networks
State-approved academic research
Authorized foreign media with government press credentials
laws.sourceLabel: Freedom House — Cuba Freedom on the Net 2023

quiz.q: What did Cuba's Decree 370 of 2019 prohibit?
options: Content contrary to social interest and public morals
quiz.explanation: Decree 370 of 2019 prohibits publishing content 'contrary to social interest, ethics, and public morals' — a broad provision used to restrict criticism of the government online.

laws.title: Cuban Private Property Restrictions — Market Reforms After Decades of Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Cuba only legalized private home sales in 2011; small businesses re-legalized; major reforms ongoing
laws.fullDescription: Cuba maintained near-total prohibition on private property transactions for decades after the 1959 revolution. The 2011 Raúl Castro reforms legalized home sales and purchases for the first time since the 1960s — Cubans can now buy and sell one primary and one vacation home. Small private businesses (cuentapropistas) were re-legalized in 2011, expanded significantly in 2021 to include Medium, Small, and Micro Enterprises (MiPyMEs). Cubans can now legally own small businesses in most sectors (but not media). Foreign investment requires state joint ventures. The US dollar was re-legalized (partially) in 2019 for state stores. Despite reforms, the dual-currency system created severe distortions — the official exchange rate vs. informal rate diverged dramatically. The 2021 monetary unification (tarea ordenamiento) triggered inflation exceeding 500%.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized use of state property for private commercial purposes: confiscation + fines + criminal charges. Operating unlicensed businesses: fines + business closure. Currency speculation: 2–8 years imprisonment.
exceptions: State-approved MiPyMEs in licensed sectors
Farmers on cooperative land have production rights (not ownership)
Diplomatic and foreign resident housing follows different rules
laws.sourceLabel: Cuban Official Gazette — Private Sector Reform Decrees 2011-2021

quiz.q: When did Cuba legalize private home sales for the first time since the 1959 revolution?
quiz.explanation: Cuba legalized private home sales in 2011 under Raúl Castro's economic reforms — ending a 50-year prohibition. Before 2011, Cubans could only swap homes (permuta) but not sell them for money. The 2011 reforms also re-legalized small private businesses after decades of state economic monopoly.

laws.title: Cuban Son and Salsa Cultural Heritage — UNESCO Recognition and State-Controlled Music Industry
laws.subtitle: Cuba's musical traditions are UNESCO recognized; the state controls music education and performance rights
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's music — son cubano, rumba, mambo, and salsa — was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage (Cuban Rumba, 2016; Traditional Cuban Music, under consideration). The Cuban Institute of Music (ICM) and the UNEAC (Union of Cuban Writers and Artists) manage the country's music industry. Musicians must be registered with these state bodies to perform professionally or record music. Earnings from international performances are partially remitted to the Cuban state. The Buena Vista Social Club recordings (1996, Ry Cooder collaborations) brought international attention but also raised questions about artists' compensation — Cuban musicians received minimal payment compared to the album's global success. Cultural performances require Ministry of Culture authorization. The state selectively allows some traditional music to be performed commercially for tourism.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized professional music performances without ICM/UNEAC registration: fines + confiscation of earnings. Organizing unauthorized concerts: administrative sanctions. Copyright violations: fines under Cuban IP law.
exceptions: Amateur community performances at neighborhood level (CDR-organized events)
Religious ceremonial music within Santería ceremonies
Academic music education performances at authorized conservatories

quiz.q: What Cuban musical genre was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016?
quiz.explanation: Cuban Rumba — an Afro-Cuban musical and dance tradition involving call-and-response singing, percussion, and improvised dance — was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016. The inscription recognized rumba as a cornerstone of Cuban cultural identity rooted in African traditions brought to Cuba during slavery.

laws.title: Total Grid Collapse & Energy Crisis 2024
laws.subtitle: Cuba's electrical grid suffered complete nationwide failures in October 2024
laws.fullDescription: In October 2024, Cuba's national electrical grid collapsed entirely — multiple times — leaving the entire island of 11 million people without power for days at a stretch. The crisis, caused by decades of underinvestment, fuel shortages due to U.S. sanctions, and inability to maintain Soviet-era infrastructure, triggered the largest protests since 2021. The government declared a 'special period in time of peace' and rationed fuel. Cubans faced 12–20 hour daily blackouts even before the total collapse. Hundreds of thousands have emigrated since 2021; remittances — not sugar or tobacco — are now the main source of foreign currency.
laws.penalty: Protesting the blackouts: risk of detention under Decree 349 and anti-protest laws. 2021 protest participants received sentences of 5–25 years. Critical social media posts: criminal charges under cybercrime regulations.
exceptions: Medical facilities receive priority power allocation
Party officials and tourist zones receive preferential power
Cubans with solar panels — increasingly common among those who can afford them — have partial independence

quiz.q: What triggered major protests in Cuba in October 2024?
options: Complete nationwide electrical grid collapse leaving the island without power
quiz.explanation: Cuba's complete national electrical grid collapse in October 2024, leaving all 11 million Cubans without power for days, triggered widespread protests — the worst energy crisis in Cuba's history resulting from decades of underinvestment and fuel shortages.

laws.title: Private Enterprise Legalization 2021
laws.subtitle: Cuba legalized small and medium private businesses for the first time since 1968 revolutionized the economy
laws.fullDescription: In August 2021, Cuba legalized small and medium private enterprises (MIPYMES — micro, small and medium enterprises) for the first time since the socialist revolution of 1968 eliminated virtually all private business. Over 10,000 private businesses were registered in the first year, primarily in food, retail, and services. The reform was driven partly by economic necessity — the COVID-19 pandemic collapsed tourism, and the economy contracted 11% in 2020. Private paladares (restaurants) and casas particulares (B&Bs) had existed in gray zones since the 1990s 'Special Period,' but formal legal recognition was new. By 2023, economic crisis overwhelmed the nascent private sector as power cuts, supply shortages, and inflation persisted.
laws.penalty: Operating a business without registration: fines and forced closure. Tax evasion by registered businesses: fines and criminal prosecution. Import of goods for unauthorized resale (black market): criminal charges.
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives have a separate legal framework predating MIPYMES
Cultural workers (artists, musicians) have a separate self-employment framework
Foreign joint ventures are governed by separate foreign investment laws

quiz.q: Since which year had Cuba effectively banned private businesses before the 2021 MIPYMES legalization?
quiz.explanation: Cuba banned virtually all private businesses in 1968 when Fidel Castro's 'Revolutionary Offensive' nationalized the remaining small private enterprises — making the 2021 legalization of MIPYMES the first formal recognition of small private businesses in over 50 years.

laws.title: Cuba's 11J Protests & Internet Shutdown Laws
laws.subtitle: Cuba's July 2021 mass protests — sparked by WhatsApp and Facebook — led to the country's first organized internet blackout
laws.fullDescription: On July 11, 2021 ('11J'), Cubans across the island took to the streets in the largest protests since 1994 — chanting 'Patria y Vida' (Homeland and Life) and 'Libertad' (Freedom). The protests were organized largely through social media. The government responded by cutting mobile internet access — one of the first documented national internet shutdowns in Latin America. Over 1,400 protesters were arrested; more than 700 received prison sentences of up to 25 years for charges of 'sedition' and 'public disorder.' The protests exposed the depth of public discontent over food and medicine shortages, power outages, and political repression that had intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic.
laws.penalty: 'Sedition': up to 25 years imprisonment. 'Public disorder': up to 1 year. Peaceful protest without state authorization: criminal charges under Decree-Law 370 on online content
exceptions: State employees who participated faced additional administrative penalties including job loss
Some defendants received conditional sentences or pardons under family pressure campaigns

quiz.q: What was the name of the protest song that became the anthem of Cuba's July 2021 uprising?
quiz.explanation: 'Patria y Vida' (Homeland and Life) — a rap song by Cuban artists — became the anthem of the July 11, 2021 protests, its title inverting the revolutionary slogan 'Patria o Muerte' (Homeland or Death) into a demand for life and freedom.

laws.title: Cuba Legalizes Small & Medium Private Businesses (2021)
laws.subtitle: For the first time since the 1968 Revolutionary Offensive abolished private business, Cuba legally recognized small and medium-sized private enterprises
laws.fullDescription: In August 2021, Cuba adopted Decree-Law 46, legally recognizing micro, small, and medium-sized private enterprises (MiPymes) for the first time since the 1968 'Revolutionary Offensive' nationalized virtually all private businesses. By 2023, over 10,000 private businesses had been registered. The reform was driven by the economic collapse during COVID-19, remittance dependency, and the failure of state enterprises to supply basic goods. Private restaurants (paladares) had existed in a gray zone since the 1990s; the new framework formalized and expanded this. However, private businesses face access challenges: difficulty obtaining wholesale goods, hard-currency barriers, and periodic state campaigns against 'illegalities.'
laws.penalty: Operating a business without MiPymes registration: fines and business closure. Tax evasion by private businesses: fines and potential imprisonment
exceptions: Some sectors remain reserved for state enterprises — media, education, major industry
Foreign investment partnerships with state entities are governed by a separate foreign investment law

quiz.q: In what year did Cuba last have widespread private businesses before the 2021 reform?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 1968 'Revolutionary Offensive' nationalized virtually all remaining private businesses, including small shops and street vendors. The 2021 MiPymes law was the first formal legal recognition of small private businesses since that near-total nationalization 53 years earlier.

laws.title: Law Against Dissent
laws.subtitle: Cuba's Penal Code criminalizes criticism of the government
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Penal Code (2022 update) includes provisions under Articles 143–144 that criminalize 'contempt' (desacato) toward the state, its officials, or its institutions — effectively making public criticism of the government a crime. Combined with vague 'social dangerousness' (peligrosidad social) provisions, individuals can be imprisoned pre-emptively based on 'propensity' to commit crimes. The July 2021 protests saw hundreds arrested under these laws. Independent journalists, artists, and activists regularly face charges. Cuba consistently ranks among the most repressive countries for press freedom.
laws.penalty: 1 to 3 years imprisonment for desacato; up to 4 years for 'social dangerousness'; longer sentences for organized dissent
exceptions: No meaningful legal exceptions for political dissent in practice
State-approved criticism within the single-party system is permitted

quiz.q: What term describes Cuba's law allowing pre-emptive imprisonment based on 'propensity' to commit crimes?
quiz.explanation: Peligrosidad social (social dangerousness) allows Cuban authorities to imprison people who haven't committed a crime but are deemed likely to do so based on their lifestyle or associations.

laws.title: Universal Healthcare Law
laws.subtitle: Cuba's constitution guarantees free universal healthcare to all citizens
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 1976 Constitution (revised 2019) enshrines the right to free healthcare for all citizens (Article 86). Cuba's National Health System (Sistema Nacional de Salud) provides free healthcare, education, and social services. Despite the US embargo's impact on medical supplies, Cuba has produced significant medical achievements — including developing its own COVID-19 vaccines (Abdala and Soberana), eliminating mother-to-child HIV transmission (WHO certified 2015), and maintaining a doctor-to-population ratio comparable to developed nations. Cuba exports doctors to over 60 countries through its medical diplomacy program, which generates significant foreign revenue.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a right-granting provision; violations of medical professional standards carry disciplinary and criminal sanctions
exceptions: Foreign nationals may access Cuba's healthcare system through paid services (separate from the free system for Cubans)
Private medical practice was historically banned but has been gradually liberalized

quiz.q: What did the WHO certify about Cuba in 2015 regarding HIV transmission?
options: Cuba had the lowest HIV rate in the Americas
Cuba developed the first HIV vaccine
Cuba was the first country to offer free HIV treatment
quiz.explanation: In 2015, the World Health Organization certified Cuba as the first country in the world to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis — a public health achievement praised globally, even by governments critical of Cuba's political system.

laws.title: Cuban Tourism Apartheid History
laws.subtitle: Cuba's apartheid tourism system prohibited Cubans from hotels — laws repealed in 2008
laws.fullDescription: From 1993 to 2008, Cuba maintained a two-tier system: hotels, beaches, and tourist facilities operated exclusively in US dollars and were off-limits to Cuban citizens, who were legally restricted to peso-economy services. This 'tourist apartheid' (sometimes called 'Tourism Apartheid' in academic literature) was enforced under resolutions from the Ministry of Tourism. Raúl Castro repealed these restrictions in 2008, allowing Cubans to book hotels and use tourist facilities. However, the dual currency system (CUC and CUP) maintained economic separation until the 2021 currency unification. The legacy of the system remains in tourism pricing structures that effectively exclude most Cubans.
laws.penalty: Under the historic system: Cubans found in tourist areas faced police questioning; hotel staff who assisted Cubans: dismissal
exceptions: The restrictions were repealed in 2008 — they no longer apply

quiz.q: In what year did Cuba repeal its law preventing Cuban citizens from using tourist hotels?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Raúl Castro repealed the restrictions preventing Cuban citizens from using tourist hotels and facilities in 2008 — ending a 15-year period of 'tourism apartheid' in which Cubans were legally excluded from dollar-economy services on their own island.

laws.title: Family Code 2022 (Código de las Familias)
laws.subtitle: Cuba's new Family Code legalized same-sex marriage and surrogacy through a national referendum
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's new Family Code, approved by national referendum on September 25, 2022, with 66.9% voting yes, is one of the most progressive family laws in Latin America and the Caribbean. The Code: legalizes same-sex marriage (Cuba became the 33rd country globally); establishes rights for same-sex couples to adopt; creates legal frameworks for gestational surrogacy; strengthens protections against domestic violence; recognizes polyamorous family structures for property and inheritance purposes; and expands the definition of 'family' to include non-biological relationships. The Code replaced the 1975 Family Code from the early revolutionary period. Notably, Cuba — a communist single-party state — passed this through a democratic referendum, partially to demonstrate the state's alignment with its younger population. The Catholic Church and evangelical groups opposed it. Implementation has faced bureaucratic challenges.
laws.penalty: Domestic violence penalties were strengthened under the new code; same-sex couples have equal rights and protections under family law; surrogacy violations: civil and criminal liability
exceptions: Religious institutions retain autonomy in their internal practices
Foreign nationals' family relationships governed by applicable bilateral treaties
Pre-existing adoptions under old code are grandfathered

laws.title: Cryptocurrency Legalization and Digital Payment Law
laws.subtitle: Cuba legalized cryptocurrency payments in 2021 partly to circumvent US financial sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Central Bank Resolution 215/2021 (August 2021) authorized the use of cryptocurrencies in commercial transactions within Cuba, becoming one of the first countries to nationally legalize cryptocurrency use partly as a strategy to circumvent US financial sanctions (which block Cuba from the traditional dollar banking system). Cuba also developed plans for a digital peso (moneda digital) through the Banco Central de Cuba (BCC). The authorization allowed Cuban businesses to accept Bitcoin, USDT, and other cryptocurrencies from customers and from the Cuban diaspora sending remittances. US financial sanctions make dollar remittances difficult; cryptocurrency offered a workaround. Cuba's internet penetration (approximately 70% mobile coverage) limited widespread adoption. The government simultaneously extended its control over private businesses through Resolution 42/2021 creating 'Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises' (MiPyMEs) with private ownership rights — a significant economic opening — while maintaining overall communist framework.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized cryptocurrency operations outside BCC-approved parameters: administrative sanctions; money laundering using cryptocurrency: criminal prosecution; foreign exchange control violations: fines
exceptions: State enterprises have separate foreign exchange frameworks
Dollar remittances remain possible through formal channels in limited amounts
The embargo creates de facto exemptions from US cryptocurrency restrictions in practice

laws.title: National Power Grid Collapse and Energy Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cuba's electrical grid failed nationwide, accelerating emigration
laws.fullDescription: In October 2024, Cuba experienced a near-total national power grid collapse, leaving the island's 11 million people without electricity for days. The blackout followed chronic power shortages that had plagued Cuba for years, with rolling outages of 12-20 hours daily. The crisis stems from aging Soviet-era infrastructure, US sanctions blocking fuel imports, and economic mismanagement under the state energy monopoly Unión Eléctrica. Cuba's population has shrunk significantly due to emigration — over 500,000 Cubans entered the US in 2022-2023 alone. The Communist Party blamed sabotage and sanctions; critics pointed to structural economic failures.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized electricity use or tapping grid: up to 8 years imprisonment under Penal Code. Black market fuel trading: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Hospitals and critical infrastructure given priority power access
Foreign tourist facilities have separate generator backup systems

quiz.q: What caused Cuba's October 2024 nationwide power grid collapse?
options: A combination of aging infrastructure, fuel shortages, and economic mismanagement
A deliberate shutdown for grid maintenance
Sabotage by foreign actors confirmed by international investigation
quiz.explanation: Cuba's grid collapse resulted from decades of underinvestment in aging Soviet-era infrastructure, combined with chronic fuel shortages worsened by US sanctions and economic mismanagement.

laws.title: Cuba's Internet Controls and VPN Cat-and-Mouse
laws.subtitle: Cuba expanded internet access but tightened censorship and prosecuted online dissent
laws.fullDescription: Cuba expanded mobile internet access in 2018 — the last major country to do so — but simultaneously maintained strict control over content. The government regularly blocks social media during protests (as in July 2021 when the largest protests since 1959 erupted). Resolution 105/2021 imposed licensing requirements on online media and criminalized 'destabilizing' content. Despite official blocking of platforms like Twitter and Facebook during unrest, VPN usage surged — Cuba's telecom monopoly ETECSA has throttled VPN traffic. Journalists and activists have been prosecuted for social media posts under broadly worded laws against 'enemy propaganda' and 'disrespect for authorities.' The 2023 Penal Code expanded digital offenses.
laws.penalty: Anti-government social media posts: up to 4 years under 'disrespect for authorities' law. Enemy propaganda online: up to 8 years. Operating unlicensed online media: 5 years.
exceptions: Foreign journalists with accreditation may use encrypted communications with reduced risk
Tourism-related social media promotion tolerated

quiz.q: When did Cuba finally provide mobile internet access to its citizens?
options: 2008, during the Obama era communications easing
2018, making it one of the last countries to do so
2022, after the July 2021 protests forced the government's hand
quiz.explanation: Cuba provided mobile internet access to its citizens in December 2018, making it one of the last countries in the world to do so — while simultaneously maintaining strict content censorship and blocking platforms during protests.

laws.title: Cuba's Electricity Rationing and Public Anger
laws.subtitle: Cuba implemented severe electricity rationing with power outages exceeding 20 hours daily
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's electricity crisis, which peaked with the October 2024 national blackout, became entrenched through 2024-2025. Rationing of 16-20 hours daily has become normalized in most provinces. The aging thermoelectric plants — burning expensive imported fuel oil from Russia, Venezuela, and Algeria — fail regularly. Cuba's domestic oil production has declined. The government has struggled to fund emergency generator fuel purchases amid the US trade embargo and its own fiscal crisis. The crisis has accelerated emigration (over 500,000 Cubans entered the US in 2022-2023 via various pathways). Hospitals and food storage facilities face critical power shortages. Public protests — rare in Cuba — have occurred, with 'Patria y Vida' becoming an anthem of discontent.
laws.penalty: Public protest against government energy policy: up to 10 years under 'social dangerousness' provisions. Spreading 'enemy propaganda' about power outages: up to 8 years.
exceptions: Essential services (hospitals, diplomatic facilities) maintain priority power allocation
Private solar installations permitted but materials scarce and expensive

quiz.q: How many hours per day have many Cubans experienced electricity rationing in 2024-2025?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's electricity rationing reached 16-20 hours daily in most provinces by 2024-2025 — with the October 2024 national blackout being the peak, when the entire country lost power for days due to grid collapse.

laws.title: Cuba's Law 389 and Private Business Expansion
laws.subtitle: Cuba cautiously expands private sector while criminalizing dissent
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2021 constitutional reforms and subsequent legislation (including allowing private micro, small, and medium enterprises — MiPyMEs) represented the most significant opening of the Cuban economy since the Special Period. By 2023, over 8,000 private businesses had been registered. However, the economic liberalization coincided with intensified repression of dissent following the July 11, 2021 protests — the largest in Cuba in decades. Hundreds of protesters received sentences of 6-25 years. Cuba's Law 389 on Cybersecurity criminalizes online speech deemed threatening to the state. Internet outages during protests are common.
laws.penalty: Participating in anti-government protests: up to 25 years for 'sedition.' Spreading anti-government content online: up to 8 years. Foreign-funded political activity: up to 10 years. Operating unauthorized business (non-registered): fines and asset confiscation
exceptions: Self-employed workers (cuentapropistas) in approved categories allowed to operate
Agricultural cooperatives have special legal status
Religious organizations maintain some autonomy for internal activities

quiz.q: What sparked Cuba's largest protests in decades on July 11, 2021?
options: Economic hardship, food shortages, and power cuts amid COVID-19
quiz.explanation: Cuba's July 11, 2021 protests — the largest in decades — were sparked by economic hardship, food and medicine shortages, and power cuts during COVID-19, leading to rare public criticism of the government which responded with mass arrests and long prison sentences.

laws.title: Cuba's Energy Crisis and Nationwide Blackouts
laws.subtitle: Cuba's electrical grid collapses as fuel shortages cause total blackouts
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced catastrophic electrical grid failures in October 2024 when the entire national grid collapsed, leaving all 11 million Cubans without power for days. The outage resulted from a combination of decades of infrastructure decay, fuel shortages preventing thermal power plants from running, Hurricane Oscar making landfall during the crisis, and the economic collapse of the state energy monopoly UNE. The Cuban government requested emergency aid from Russia, Venezuela, and Mexico. Cuba's Special Period-era energy laws remained in effect but could not be enforced given total grid failure. The crisis intensified migration flows as Cubans fled the island.
laws.penalty: Sabotage of electrical infrastructure: up to 20 years imprisonment. Stealing electrical cable (common during crisis): up to 10 years. Spreading 'disinformation' about the energy crisis: up to 8 years under cybercrime law. Black market fuel sales: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Hospitals maintained generator backup power under emergency protocols
Diplomatic missions maintained their own generator power
Critical infrastructure workers exempt from curfew during restoration efforts

quiz.q: What year did Cuba experience a catastrophic total national grid collapse?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's entire national electrical grid collapsed in October 2024, leaving all 11 million Cubans without power for days — the result of decades of infrastructure decay, fuel shortages, and Hurricane Oscar hitting during the crisis.

laws.title: Private Business Licensing and New Economic Reforms
laws.subtitle: Cuba's 2021 reforms authorized private SMEs for the first time in decades
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2021 economic reforms formally authorized small and medium enterprises (MiPyMES) for the first time in decades, allowing private businesses with up to 100 employees. By 2024, tens of thousands of private businesses had registered. However, private businesses face restrictions on imports, foreign currency, and certain sectors. The Cuban government retains control of strategic sectors (telecommunications, energy, education, healthcare). Black market activity and operating without a license remain criminal offenses. Foreign investment requires joint ventures with state entities in most sectors. The legal framework for private business continues to evolve rapidly.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed business: fines and asset confiscation; tax evasion: imprisonment up to 8 years
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives have separate legal framework
Self-employment (trabajo por cuenta propia) has different rules than MiPyMES

quiz.q: What did Cuba's 2021 economic reforms authorize for the first time in decades?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2021 reforms formally authorized private small and medium enterprises (MiPyMES) for the first time in decades, allowing private businesses with up to 100 employees.

laws.title: 2023-2024 Energy Crisis and Civil Unrest Laws
laws.subtitle: Cuba criminalized civil protests during its worst energy crisis in decades
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced its worst energy crisis in decades in 2023-2024, with nationwide power outages lasting 12-20 hours daily. Severe food shortages compounded the crisis. Small protests erupted, and the government responded by arresting demonstrators under laws prohibiting public disorder and 'acts against state security.' Cuba's Law 88 (Protection of Independence and the National Economy) and Act 370 (electronic communications) were used to prosecute social media users documenting the crisis. Several protesters received multi-year sentences. The energy crisis was attributed to aging Soviet-era power plants and US sanctions. Cuba requested UN emergency humanitarian assistance.
laws.penalty: Public disorder during protests: 1–10 years imprisonment; distributing 'enemy propaganda': up to 8 years under Law 88
exceptions: Government-authorized marches in support of the revolution are permitted
Religious services at licensed churches

quiz.q: What laws did Cuba use to prosecute social media users documenting the 2023-2024 energy crisis?
options: Copyright law and intellectual property acts
Law 88 and Act 370 on electronic communications
quiz.explanation: Cuba used Law 88 (Protection of Independence and National Economy) and Act 370 (electronic communications regulations) to prosecute social media users who documented the energy crisis, treating the documentation as 'enemy propaganda.'

laws.title: Migration Wave and Exit Permit Requirements
laws.subtitle: Cuba experienced its largest emigration wave in history amid economic crisis
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Migratory Law (Decree-Law 302) governs emigration. Cubans must obtain an exit permit (tarjeta blanca) for extended stays abroad, though this requirement was modified in 2013. The economic and energy crisis of 2021-2024 triggered a massive emigration wave — the largest in Cuban history, with over 600,000 Cubans arriving in the US through the US-Mexico border in fiscal year 2023. The Cuban government cannot legally prevent emigration but can revoke Cuban citizenship and property rights for those who stay abroad. Persons who left illegally (wet foot/dry foot) faced different legal consequences. The emigration wave significantly reduced Cuba's workforce.
laws.penalty: Illegal exit from Cuba: criminal prosecution and travel document confiscation; abandoning Cuban state employment abroad: loss of job and housing rights
exceptions: Professional athletes and artists on state-approved tours have specific return obligations
Persons with family medical emergencies may receive emergency exit permissions

quiz.q: Approximately how many Cubans arrived in the US through the border in fiscal year 2023?
quiz.explanation: Over 600,000 Cubans arrived in the US through the US-Mexico border in fiscal year 2023 — the largest Cuban emigration wave in history, driven by the severe economic and energy crisis on the island.

laws.title: Cuba New Penal Code and Political Dissent Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Cuba's 2022 Penal Code expands crimes against the state
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's new Penal Code, which came into force in December 2022, significantly expanded criminal categories related to dissent and destabilization. It introduced broader definitions of sedition, treason, and spreading false information, with penalties up to 30 years for organizing protests or communicating with foreign media. Following the July 2021 protests, over 1,000 demonstrators were prosecuted under old and new laws, with sentences up to 25 years.
laws.penalty: Imprisonment from 4 years for minor dissent to 30 years for organizing protests deemed seditious; capital punishment for terrorism
exceptions: State-approved religious activity
State-sponsored cultural expression
Activities by foreign diplomats within treaty rights

quiz.q: What maximum prison term can Cuban dissidents face under the 2022 Penal Code for organizing protests?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2022 Penal Code expanded criminalization of dissent with penalties up to 30 years for organizing protests deemed seditious or destabilizing to the state.

laws.title: Cuba Energy Crisis and Emergency Economic Laws
laws.subtitle: Cuba enacts emergency measures amid severe power and fuel shortages
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has faced its worst energy crisis in decades, with rolling blackouts of 20 or more hours per day in 2024. The government enacted emergency economic decrees allowing foreign companies to invest in electricity generation, expanded barter arrangements for fuel, and created special regimes for energy investment. Cuba also imposed significant restrictions on fuel use, cutting state vehicle fuel allocations and limiting private transport. Despite emergency measures, the crisis has driven record emigration.
laws.penalty: Violations of fuel rationing rules: administrative penalties and fines; illegal fuel trading: criminal prosecution up to 5 years
exceptions: Hospitals and emergency services receive priority fuel allocation
Food production and transport receive exemptions
Diplomatic missions operate under their own fuel arrangements

quiz.q: How severe were Cuba's power blackouts at their worst in 2024?
quiz.explanation: Cuba experienced rolling blackouts of 20 or more hours per day during its worst energy crisis in decades in 2024, driving emergency economic legislation and record emigration.

laws.title: Cuba Criminal Code Application to 2021 Protesters
laws.subtitle: Cuba sentences July 2021 protesters to long prison terms
laws.fullDescription: Trials of participants in Cuba's historic July 11, 2021 protests concluded with sentences ranging from months to 25 years in prison for the most serious cases. The Supreme Court upheld most sentences. The protests, which spread to over 40 cities, were the largest demonstrations in Cuba since 1959. Charges included sedition, public disorder, and attacks on state security. International human rights organizations documented over 1,000 arrests and called the prosecutions politically motivated.
laws.penalty: Sedition: up to 25 years; public disorder: up to 4 years; attacking state security: up to 10 years; spreading enemy propaganda: up to 8 years
exceptions: Minors (under 18) were tried separately in juvenile system
Those who recanted publicly received reduced sentences in some cases
Medical personnel arrested during protests had their cases reviewed separately

quiz.q: What were Cuba's July 2021 protests notable for in the island's history?
options: The largest demonstrations in Cuba since the revolution in 1959
First protests supported by the government
quiz.explanation: Cuba's July 11, 2021 protests, which spread to over 40 cities, were the largest popular demonstrations in Cuba since the 1959 revolution, resulting in over 1,000 arrests and sentences of up to 25 years for participants.

laws.title: Internet and VPN Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Cuba's controls on internet access and circumvention tools
laws.fullDescription: Cuba maintains strict controls on internet access and prohibits the use of VPNs and other tools to circumvent government content filtering. Internet access is monitored, and accessing blocked content using circumvention tools is illegal. Social media platforms have been intermittently blocked during periods of civil unrest. The government operates through ETECSA, the sole telecommunications provider, which monitors traffic. Mobile internet is available but expensive relative to local wages.
laws.penalty: Using VPNs or circumvention tools can result in fines and detention; spreading content deemed subversive via internet carries sentences of 2 to 8 years
exceptions: Approved research institutions may access restricted content
Diplomatic missions have separate internet infrastructure
Medical facilities have special access provisions

quiz.q: Who is the sole telecommunications provider controlling internet access in Cuba?
quiz.explanation: ETECSA (Empresa de Telecomunicaciones de Cuba) is the state monopoly telecommunications provider that controls all internet infrastructure in Cuba.

laws.title: Small and Medium Enterprise Legalization
laws.subtitle: Cuba's recognition of private business for the first time since 1968
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted legislation recognizing small and medium enterprises (SMEs) as a legal business form for the first time since the elimination of private business in 1968. Cubans can now legally register private companies employing up to 100 workers, access bank accounts, and operate in most sectors of the economy (with some state monopolies excluded). The reform followed the expansion of self-employment categories. Foreign investment in private Cuban companies is also being explored. The reforms represent a significant departure from Cuba's planned economy model, though the state sector remains dominant.
laws.penalty: Unregistered businesses face fines and business closure orders; tax evasion by registered SMEs carries back taxes plus 100% penalty; unauthorized imports for business use carry confiscation
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives have separate legal framework predating the SME reform
Self-employed individuals (cuentapropistas) remain under the existing self-employment regime
State enterprises are not subject to SME regulations

quiz.q: Up to how many workers can Cuban SMEs legally employ under the new legislation?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's SME legislation allows private companies to employ up to 100 workers, a significant departure from the previous system that only allowed very small-scale self-employment activities.

laws.title: Energy Crisis Legal Measures
laws.subtitle: Cuba's emergency laws managing acute electricity shortages
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced its worst energy crisis in decades in 2024, with power outages lasting 20 or more hours daily in many provinces. The government's aging thermoelectric plants repeatedly failed, and fuel shortages compounded the problem. Emergency measures included mandatory reduced consumption targets for businesses and households, fuel rationing, legal restrictions on unauthorized generators and fuel use that competed with the official supply, and criminal penalties for stealing electricity from the grid. Rolling blackouts became the new normal and triggered rare public protests.
laws.penalty: Electricity theft from the grid carries 2 to 5 years imprisonment; fuel hoarding during rationing periods carries fines and confiscation; unauthorized electricity resale carries criminal charges
exceptions: Hospitals and essential services receive priority electricity allocation
Agricultural food production facilities receive uninterrupted supply where possible
Schools receive partial priority for evening study hours
laws.sourceLabel: Cuban Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: How long were power outages lasting in many Cuban provinces during the 2024 energy crisis?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2024 energy crisis was severe enough that many provinces experienced 20 or more hours of daily power outages as the country's aging thermoelectric infrastructure repeatedly failed and fuel shortages prevented adequate generation.

laws.title: Cuba Energy Crisis Emergency Measures
laws.subtitle: Nationwide blackouts prompt rationing and emergency energy laws
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted emergency energy rationing decrees in 2024–2025 as the island faced its worst electricity crisis in decades, with rolling blackouts lasting 18–20 hours daily in some provinces. The measures authorized the state energy company (UNE) to implement mandatory consumption limits for businesses and households, prioritize hospitals and food storage, and impose fines for unauthorized power generation. Fuel shortages compounded the crisis as Venezuela reduced oil deliveries.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized use of generators above permitted wattage: fines of 2,000–5,000 Cuban pesos. Commercial establishments violating rationing orders face temporary closure.
exceptions: Hospitals and medical facilities exempt from rationing
Diplomatic residences and foreign-operated facilities receive differentiated supply
Food storage facilities with perishable goods receive priority allocation

quiz.q: What was the approximate daily blackout duration in worst-affected Cuban provinces during the 2024-2025 energy crisis?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's energy crisis resulted in rolling blackouts of 18–20 hours per day in the worst-affected provinces, as the state electricity company implemented severe rationing due to fuel shortages and aging infrastructure.

laws.title: Cuba Mass Emigration Crisis and Migration Agreement
laws.subtitle: Record outflows as economic collapse drives exodus
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced its largest emigration wave in history in 2022–2024, with over 500,000 people leaving — approximately 4.5% of the population — primarily via the US-Mexico border using the humanitarian parole program. The crisis prompted bilateral US-Cuba discussions on migration management, including agreements to accept Cuban nationals removed from the US and to resume legal migration pathways. Cuba enacted laws restricting emigration of professionals (especially doctors) under multi-year service contracts.
laws.penalty: Cuban government employees who emigrate without authorization while under service contracts face property confiscation and career bans. Unauthorized exit by military or security personnel: criminal prosecution for desertion.
exceptions: Cubans who obtain US legal immigrant visas through family reunification or diversity lottery subject to normal emigration procedures
Artists and athletes may apply for temporary exit permits for cultural and sporting events

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Cuba's population emigrated in the record 2022-2024 wave?
quiz.explanation: Over 500,000 Cubans emigrated in 2022-2024, representing approximately 4.5% of Cuba's population — the largest emigration wave in the country's history, driven by economic collapse, power outages, and political repression.

laws.title: Cuba Constitutional Crisis and Succession Planning
laws.subtitle: Power transfer as Raúl Castro era ends
laws.fullDescription: Cuba faced mounting pressure from its intertwined political and economic crises in 2024–2025. President Miguel Díaz-Canel and the Communist Party struggled with the country's worst crisis since the Special Period of the 1990s: fuel shortages, power outages, mass emigration, and economic contraction. The aging leadership — Raúl Castro turned 93 in 2024 — raised questions about succession in a system with no democratic transfer mechanism. The National Assembly approved emergency economic measures including modest market reforms for small businesses.
laws.penalty: Political opposition activity outside the Communist Party framework: criminal prosecution under Cuba's Code of Social Defense for 'pre-criminal dangerousness,' fines and imprisonment of 1–4 years. Organizing unauthorized public gatherings: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Small-scale private business operators (cuentapropistas) retain legal status for permitted activities
Religious organizations registered with the Religious Affairs Office may hold services without direct state supervision

quiz.q: How old did Raúl Castro turn in 2024, raising succession questions in Cuba?
quiz.explanation: Raúl Castro turned 93 in 2024, raising questions about succession planning in Cuba's Communist system that lacks democratic transfer mechanisms. The aging leadership, combined with Cuba's worst economic crisis since the 1990s Special Period, intensified concerns about the country's political stability.

laws.title: Energy Emergency Decree and Blackout Management
laws.subtitle: Government emergency powers over electricity rationing during crisis
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted emergency decrees granting the government authority to implement rolling blackouts of up to 20 hours per day in response to fuel shortages and power plant failures. The decrees also criminalized unauthorized fuel resale and established priority electricity allocation to hospitals, food production, and water pumping. Citizens who tampered with meters or used illegal generators faced prison terms.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized fuel resale: up to 8 years; meter tampering: up to 4 years; illegal commercial generator use: fines
exceptions: Medical facilities receive uninterrupted power
Food storage facilities given priority allocation

quiz.q: Why did Cuba enact electricity rationing emergency decrees?
options: Due to fuel shortages and power plant failures
To comply with international energy agreements
quiz.explanation: Cuba's energy emergency decrees were prompted by severe fuel shortages and aging power plant failures that caused widespread blackouts across the island.

laws.title: Military Courts for Civilian Protesters
laws.subtitle: Cuba uses military tribunals to prosecute July 11 protest participants
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's government used military courts to prosecute civilians arrested during the July 11, 2021 mass protests — the largest in decades. Sentences ranged from months to over 25 years for charges including sedition. The use of military tribunals for civilians drew international condemnation. Amnesty International designated many prisoners as prisoners of conscience.
laws.penalty: Sedition charges: up to 30 years; 'public disorder': up to 10 years; 'contempt' (desacato): up to 3 years
exceptions: Juveniles tried in separate youth justice system with lighter sentences
Those who signed loyalty pledges received suspended sentences in some cases

quiz.q: What was unusual about Cuba's prosecution of July 11, 2021 protest participants?
options: Civilians were prosecuted in military courts
All charges were dropped on appeal
International observers were allowed to attend
quiz.explanation: Cuba controversially used military tribunals to prosecute civilians arrested during the July 11 protests, which international human rights organisations condemned as a denial of due process rights.

laws.title: Foreign Investment in Private Business Legalisation
laws.subtitle: Cuba expands private sector and foreign investment rights
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted reforms expanding the legal private sector to include medium-sized enterprises (mipymes) for the first time since the Revolution. Foreign investors could partner with Cuban private businesses rather than only state enterprises. The reforms were driven by economic desperation as remittances and tourism collapsed. However, the state retained strategic sector control and private businesses faced significant operational constraints.
laws.penalty: Businesses operating outside approved private sector categories: administrative fines and forced closure
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives have special status separate from new mipymes framework
Joint ventures with state enterprises continue under the existing foreign investment law

quiz.q: What type of business entity did Cuba legalise for the first time since the Revolution?
quiz.explanation: Cuba legalised medium-sized private enterprises (mipymes — micro, small, and medium enterprises) for the first time since the Revolution, allowing Cubans to operate larger private businesses and receive foreign partnerships.

laws.title: Cuba Free Trade Zone and Special Economic Zone Expansion
laws.subtitle: Cuba expands market zones amid economic collapse
laws.fullDescription: Cuba expanded its Special Development Zones (most notably Mariel Port) and created new legal frameworks enabling foreign investors to fully own companies in approved zones. The measures were driven by economic desperation — Cuba was experiencing chronic fuel shortages, food shortages, blackouts, and mass emigration. Foreign investment provided hard currency while limiting ideological concessions to pure market economics.
laws.penalty: Businesses operating outside approved zone structures: subject to nationalisation risk; currency violations in non-authorised zones: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Tourism sector companies have separate investment frameworks predating the new SEZ laws
Foreign embassies conduct commerce under diplomatic protocol separate from investment law

quiz.q: What is the name of Cuba's main Special Development Zone that has attracted significant foreign investment?
quiz.explanation: The Mariel Port Special Development Zone is Cuba's flagship foreign investment zone, designed to attract foreign companies with more liberal regulations than the rest of Cuba while maintaining state control over the broader economy.

laws.title: Cuba Energy Crisis Emergency Decrees and Economic Reform
laws.subtitle: Legal response to prolonged electrical grid collapse
laws.fullDescription: Cuba issued a series of emergency economic decrees in 2025 following the near-total electrical grid collapse that left the island in darkness for weeks in late 2024. The Emergency Economic Resilience Decree authorizes private investment in electricity generation for the first time, allows foreign companies to own up to 100% stakes in renewable energy projects, legalizes peer-to-peer energy trading between private generators, decriminalizes possession of diesel generators above previously restricted capacity, and accelerates the USD/MLC dual currency unification process. The decrees represented the most significant economic liberalization since the 1990s 'Special Period' reforms.
laws.penalty: Illegal fuel hoarding above emergency regulations: 10 years imprisonment; sabotage of electrical infrastructure: 25 years; unauthorized electricity resale at price-gouging rates: property confiscation plus 8 years
exceptions: Hospitals and essential services receive priority fuel allocation exempt from hoarding rules
Solar panel imports for residential use temporarily exempt from import duties
Agricultural cooperatives may generate and use electricity without commercial licensing

quiz.q: What significant economic change for the electricity sector did Cuba's 2025 emergency decrees introduce for the first time?
options: Allowing private investment in electricity generation
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2025 emergency energy decrees authorized private investment in electricity generation for the first time, a major liberalization allowing foreign companies full ownership of renewable energy projects.

laws.title: Cuba Internet Access Expansion and Economic Liberalization
laws.subtitle: Partial digital opening amid economic crisis
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted the Digital Economy and Internet Access Partial Liberalization Act 2025, responding to the dual crises of the 2024 electrical grid collapse and growing economic desperation. The law authorizes private internet service providers for the first time, allows private citizens to resell international roaming data packages (previously prohibited), creates a licensing framework for Cuban entrepreneurs to offer digital services internationally from Cuba, establishes the Cuban Digital Economy Zone in Havana's Miramar district with preferential regulations for tech startups, and introduces cryptocurrency acceptance in foreign-facing tourism and restaurant sectors. The reforms stopped short of freedom of expression guarantees that opposition and international observers demanded.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized ISP operation: 10 years imprisonment; digital service operating outside licensed zone: 8 years; cryptocurrency use outside permitted sectors: asset confiscation plus 5 years
exceptions: Academic internet access at universities remains under institutional rather than individual licensing
Diplomatic missions retain unrestricted internet access under Vienna Convention
Medical and pharmaceutical research has broadened internet access framework

quiz.q: What new type of private enterprise does Cuba's 2025 Digital Economy Act authorize for the first time?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Digital Economy and Internet Access Act authorizes private internet service providers for the first time — a significant liberalization in a country where internet access had been exclusively state-controlled, driven by economic crisis and the 2024 electricity grid collapse.

laws.title: Cuba Freedom of Assembly Emergency Restrictions and Protest Law
laws.subtitle: Post-2021 protest crackdown legal codification
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted the Public Order and Social Stability Protection Act 2025, codifying the crackdown frameworks used against the historic July 11, 2021 protests. The law creates new categories of 'aggravated social disorder' carrying 10-25 year sentences for organizing or participating in unauthorized assemblies that 'threaten constitutional order,' mandates criminal sentences for sharing protest footage on social media platforms, creates Special Rapid Response Courts for public order offenses with 15-day judgment timelines, establishes the Committee for Social Cohesion monitoring community compliance with socialist values, and introduces mandatory re-education programmes for convicted protesters. Human rights organizations estimated over 1,000 Cubans remained imprisoned for July 11 participation.
laws.penalty: Aggravated social disorder: 10-25 years imprisonment; protest footage sharing abroad: 5-15 years; Special Court contempt: additional 5 years; Committee non-cooperation: social benefits suspension
exceptions: State-organized demonstrations have full authorization
Funeral processions for revolutionary figures have modified assembly framework
Religious observances in registered churches have limited assembly protection

quiz.q: On what date did Cuba's historic mass protests occur that the 2025 Public Order Act's crackdown framework is based on?
quiz.explanation: July 11, 2021 saw Cuba's largest protests in decades — tens of thousands of Cubans took to the streets across the island chanting 'Libertad' (Freedom) and 'Patria y Vida' (Homeland and Life), prompting a severe government crackdown that the 2025 Public Order Act codifies into permanent law.

laws.title: Economic Crisis Emergency Powers and Rationing Act
laws.subtitle: Power blackouts, fuel shortages, and exodus legislation
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted emergency economic management legislation amid its worst economic crisis in decades, characterized by near-daily power blackouts lasting 12-20 hours, fuel shortages, food scarcity, and a massive emigration wave. The law expands state rationing authority, criminalizes 'economic sabotage' including hoarding, restricts citizens' movement to prevent rural to urban migration, and establishes penalties for participation in unauthorized foreign currency markets.
laws.penalty: Economic sabotage including hoarding goods carries up to 20 years. Unauthorized foreign currency transactions carry up to 10 years. Leaving the country without authorization faces administrative penalties and loss of state benefits.
exceptions: Medical professionals retain fuel allocations for patient transport even during severe shortages
Agricultural workers receive priority food access to maintain production

quiz.q: What basic service failure became the most visible symbol of Cuba's economic crisis?
quiz.explanation: Near-daily power blackouts lasting 12-20 hours became the defining symbol of Cuba's 2024-2025 economic crisis, triggered by fuel shortages that left the aging power grid unable to meet demand.

laws.title: Post-Díaz-Canel Leadership Succession and Economic Opening Act
laws.subtitle: Selective market opening amid regime preservation
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted limited economic liberalization legislation as the post-Díaz-Canel leadership managed the country's worst economic crisis. The law expands the private sector to allow medium-sized private businesses, creates new mechanisms for foreign investment in small businesses, partially legalizes dollar-denominated transactions, and creates a new small business registration framework. The reforms fall far short of the structural changes economists say are needed.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized private business activities outside the new framework carry up to five years imprisonment. Currency trafficking outside licensed channels carries up to three years.
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives retain their existing legal status and are not required to reregister under the new framework
US-Cuba remittance flows retain their existing humanitarian exemption pathways despite the economic crisis

quiz.q: What fundamental constraint limits the economic reforms Cuba's government is willing to make?
options: Preserving Communist Party political control while allowing limited market activity
US trade sanctions preventing any reform
quiz.explanation: Cuba's government is constrained by its determination to preserve Communist Party control. Each economic liberalization is carefully calibrated to allow enough market activity to generate revenue without creating a private sector that could challenge political power.

laws.title: Cuban Migrant Crisis and New Economic Migration Act
laws.subtitle: Managing exodus of nearly 20% of population
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted legislation addressing the massive emigration wave that has seen an estimated 500,000 to 700,000 Cubans — nearly 6-7% of the population (some estimates higher) — leave the island, primarily to the United States via the US-Cuba parole program and illegal crossings. The law modifies rules around Cubans who leave without government permission, attempts to maintain economic ties with the diaspora through remittances, and creates economic zones in border provinces.
laws.penalty: The legislation relaxes some traditional penalties for unauthorized departure, reflecting the scale of emigration making enforcement impractical. However, public dissent about emigration policy still carries risk.
exceptions: Cubans who emigrate and maintain economic ties through remittances are designated a special diaspora category with retained rights
Medical professionals who leave remain subject to the 8-year prohibition on return under the current policy

quiz.q: Approximately how many Cubans emigrated in the years 2022-2024, representing what share of the population?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 500,000 to 700,000 Cubans emigrated between 2022 and 2024 — roughly 6-7% of the island's population — making it the largest Cuban emigration wave since the Mariel boatlift. The exodus was driven by the economic crisis, power outages, and growing despair.

laws.title: Cuba Micro-Enterprise and Self-Employment Expansion Act
laws.subtitle: Private Economy Legalization Reform
laws.fullDescription: Expands Cuba's limited experiment with private enterprise by legalizing micro, small, and medium enterprises (MiPYMEs) across most economic sectors. The law allows foreign investment in Cuban private businesses, permits private companies to import and export directly, establishes limited property rights for enterprise assets, and creates a banking system for private businesses. The reforms represent the most significant economic opening since the 1959 revolution but maintain state control of strategic sectors.
laws.penalty: Administrative fines for unregistered private businesses; criminal prosecution for tax evasion
exceptions: Strategic sectors including media, defense, and education remain state monopolies
Foreign investment requires government partnership in most sectors

quiz.q: What does Cuba's Micro-Enterprise Act permit that is new for Cuban private businesses?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's act permits private companies to import and export directly for the first time, a major economic opening.

laws.title: Cuba Electricity Crisis and Energy Emergency Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Power Grid Collapse Response and Reform Law
laws.fullDescription: Responds to Cuba's catastrophic electricity crisis of 2024 when the national grid collapsed multiple times leaving the island in total blackouts for days. The law authorizes foreign investment in electricity generation, allows private energy companies for the first time, establishes emergency imports of fuel and generation equipment, creates crisis compensation mechanisms for affected businesses, and mandates grid modernization with international technical assistance.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for sabotage of power infrastructure; administrative sanctions for generating companies failing capacity commitments
exceptions: State electricity company maintains grid management authority
Military and hospital facilities have priority generation allocation

quiz.q: What unprecedented step does Cuba's Electricity Crisis Act authorize for the first time?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Electricity Crisis Act authorizes private energy companies for the first time in Cuba's socialist system, driven by the 2024 grid collapse.

laws.title: Cuba Food and Medicine Crisis Emergency Response Act
laws.subtitle: Basic Goods Shortage and Rationing Reform Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses Cuba's severe shortages of food, medicine, and fuel that have driven record emigration. The law authorizes expanded private food production and distribution, creates emergency import mechanisms for essential medicines, establishes a tiered rationing system for scarce goods, creates frameworks for remittance-funded private businesses to fill supply gaps, and establishes accountability for state enterprise failures.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for hoarding and black market profiteering during shortages
exceptions: Private food sellers may operate without full registration during emergency
Diaspora remittances for family food and medicine purchases unrestricted

quiz.q: What major consequence has Cuba's food and medicine crisis driven?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's severe shortages of food, medicine, and fuel have driven record emigration, with hundreds of thousands leaving for the United States.

laws.title: Cuba Migration Crisis and US Relations Normalization Framework Act
laws.subtitle: Emigration Rights and Diplomatic Channel Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses the massive emigration from Cuba driven by economic crisis and political repression, creating the largest Cuban diaspora since the revolution. The law creates legal emigration pathways, establishes the US-Cuba migration talks framework, creates family reunification mechanisms, and establishes protections for Cubans in the US seeking asylum.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for emigration under new framework; previous criminal prosecutions for emigration attempts reviewed
exceptions: State security and military personnel have restricted emigration
Strategic government officials require clearance before emigration

quiz.q: What has driven the massive Cuban emigration creating the largest diaspora since the revolution?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's economic crisis with severe food, medicine, and energy shortages combined with political repression have driven record emigration.

laws.title: Energy Crisis and Blackout Emergency
laws.subtitle: Cuba's Electrical Grid Collapses
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced catastrophic electrical grid failures in late 2024, with nationwide blackouts lasting days at a time. The crisis stemmed from decades of underinvestment, fuel shortages, and Soviet-era infrastructure. The failures paralyzed the economy, disrupted hospitals, and accelerated emigration. The government declared energy emergencies and sought international assistance.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for crisis; rationing and emergency measures implemented
exceptions: Medical facilities priority access
Emergency international aid accepted

quiz.q: What caused Cuba's catastrophic blackouts in 2024?
options: Decades of underinvestment and fuel shortages
quiz.explanation: Cuba's grid failures resulted from decades of underinvestment in electrical infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages, causing nationwide blackouts lasting days.

laws.title: Mass Emigration and Population Decline
laws.subtitle: Cuba Loses Record Percentage of Population
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced unprecedented mass emigration from 2021-2024, with over 500,000 Cubans — approximately 4.5% of the population — leaving primarily for the United States through the parole program and other routes. The exodus was driven by the energy crisis, economic collapse, repression, and hopelessness about the future.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for emigration; government rhetoric against emigration
exceptions: Cuban Adjustment Act provides US residency pathway
Parole programs created legal routes

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Cuba's population emigrated in 2021-2024?
quiz.explanation: Cuba lost approximately 4.5% of its population to emigration in 2021-2024, one of the largest population outflows in the country's modern history.

laws.title: Solar Energy Emergency and Grid Modernization
laws.subtitle: Cuba Pivots to Solar to Address Energy Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Following its catastrophic 2024 grid collapse, Cuba pursued emergency solar panel installations with Chinese financing, installing thousands of rooftop and ground-mounted systems. The government distributed small solar kits to families for lighting and phone charging. The pivot to solar represented a significant shift in Cuban energy policy.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; state-directed energy program
exceptions: Private business energy self-generation allowed
Distributed solar incentives

quiz.q: What country financed Cuba's emergency solar energy program?
quiz.explanation: China financed Cuba's emergency solar panel installation program following the 2024 grid collapse, with Chinese companies supplying panels and technical assistance.

laws.title: Aging Population and Demographic Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cuba's Population Shrinks From Emigration and Low Births
laws.fullDescription: Cuba faced a severe demographic crisis with a rapidly aging population, low birth rates, and mass emigration creating a population decline. Cuba became the oldest country in Latin America per capita. The healthcare system, which once provided universal coverage, struggled with doctor emigration and medicine shortages.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; government social support programs
exceptions: Remittance family support programs
Pension reform considerations

quiz.q: What demographic distinction has Cuba achieved in Latin America?
quiz.explanation: Cuba has become the oldest country in Latin America per capita due to a combination of low birth rates, aging population, and mass emigration of younger generations.

laws.title: Diplomatic Relations and Prisoner Exchanges
laws.subtitle: Cuba Participates in International Prisoner Deals
laws.fullDescription: Cuba participated in international prisoner exchange negotiations involving Russian, American, and Cuban detainees. The Biden administration briefly removed Cuba from the state sponsor of terrorism list to facilitate prisoner deals but the Trump administration relisted Cuba. Cuba maintained revolutionary posture while seeking economic relief.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; diplomatic sanctions relief sought
exceptions: US sanctions remain in force
Humanitarian exemptions

quiz.q: What did the Biden administration temporarily do to facilitate prisoner exchanges with Cuba?
options: Removed Cuba from state sponsor of terrorism list
