quiz.explanation: The Biden administration temporarily removed Cuba from the state sponsor of terrorism list as part of negotiations to facilitate prisoner exchanges.

laws.title: Energy Crisis and Blackout Emergency
laws.subtitle: Cuba faces worst power crisis since Soviet collapse with nationwide blackouts
laws.fullDescription: Cuba experienced its worst energy crisis since the 1990s Special Period following the Soviet collapse. In 2024, the national grid failed multiple times with nationwide blackouts lasting days. Cuba's thermal power plants are decrepit and fuel-dependent; Venezuela's subsidized oil deliveries have declined. The country relies on mobile generators but lacks fuel. The energy crisis compounds economic hardship from US sanctions, COVID-19 damage, and mismanagement. Hundreds of thousands have emigrated — the largest exodus since the Mariel boatlift.
laws.penalty: Energy rationing is enforced through rolling blackout schedules
exceptions: Hospitals and essential services receive priority power
Tourist hotels maintain generator backup to preserve foreign exchange earnings

laws.title: Tourism Collapse and Economic Emergency
laws.subtitle: Cuba's lifeline tourism industry fails to recover post-pandemic
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's tourism industry, which had been recovering strongly before COVID-19, collapsed and failed to fully recover. The combination of US sanctions blocking American tourists, fuel shortages preventing charter flights, hotel deterioration from lack of maintenance investment, and the overall economic crisis dramatically reduced visitor numbers. Cuba's economy depends on tourism for critical foreign exchange. Some European and Canadian tourists still visit, but numbers remain far below targets. The government has opened new private restaurants (paladares) and guesthouses (casas particulares) in a limited market opening.
laws.penalty: Private business operators must obtain licenses and pay taxes under the expanding private sector framework
exceptions: Small-scale home rentals under 3 rooms have simplified licensing
Agricultural cooperatives have separate operating framework from individual private businesses

laws.title: Largest Emigration Wave Since Revolution
laws.subtitle: Cuba loses hundreds of thousands to mass emigration
laws.fullDescription: Cuba is experiencing its largest wave of emigration since the 1959 revolution. In 2022-2023, over 500,000 Cubans entered the United States — more in two years than the previous decade. Emigrants take dangerous routes through Central America and Mexico or use the CBP One app. Cuba's economic crisis, power outages, and lack of opportunities drive the exodus. The emigration hollows out Cuba's working-age population. The US-Cuba migration agreement (wet foot/dry foot was ended in 2017) complicates the situation.
laws.penalty: Cuba restricts some citizens from emigrating by denying exit permits or passports
exceptions: Medical professionals can emigrate under bilateral health worker agreements
Cuban athletes who defect face no legal consequences from the receiving country

quiz.q: How many Cubans entered the United States in 2022-2023?
quiz.explanation: Over 500,000 Cubans entered the United States in 2022-2023 — the largest two-year migration from Cuba since the 1959 revolution — driven by economic crisis, power outages, and political repression.

laws.title: Blackouts, Exodus, and Economic System Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cuba's socialist economy facing terminal decline
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has experienced its worst economic crisis in decades, with daily blackouts lasting 12-20 hours, severe food shortages, medicine unavailability, and fuel scarcity becoming normal features of Cuban life. The electrical grid, relying on aging Soviet-era infrastructure and deteriorating oil-fired plants, has suffered cascading failures. The Cuban population has voted with its feet — over 1 million Cubans emigrated between 2021 and 2023, representing roughly 10% of the population in three years. This mass exodus drains the workforce and represents a profound rejection of the economic model. Cuba depends heavily on Venezuelan oil and remittances from the diaspora. The government has partially liberalized some small business operations but maintains state control of the commanding heights.
laws.penalty: Economic crimes including black market activity and unauthorized foreign currency transactions carry criminal penalties; political dissent is severely repressed
exceptions: State-licensed small businesses operate with somewhat more flexibility than the fully planned sector

quiz.q: Approximately how many Cubans emigrated between 2021 and 2023?
quiz.explanation: Over 1 million Cubans emigrated between 2021 and 2023 — roughly 10% of the population in three years — representing an unprecedented exodus that reflects the severity of Cuba's economic crisis.

laws.title: Internet Connectivity and Social Media Protest Suppression
laws.subtitle: Cuba controlling information in the age of social media
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's July 2021 protests — the largest since 1994 — were organized substantially through social media, particularly Facebook and WhatsApp, demonstrating how connectivity threatens authoritarian information control. The government responded by shutting down internet access during the protests. Cuba has subsequently controlled internet access more carefully, restricting speeds and access during political events. Cuba expanded mobile internet access in 2018, but it remains state-controlled through ETECSA (the monopoly telecommunications provider), and access is monitored. Social media users who post content critical of the government face prosecution. The contrast between Cuba's population (increasingly connected despite government efforts) and government's desire to control information creates persistent tension. VPN use has spread among Cubans seeking uncensored access, though the government has attempted to block VPN services.
laws.penalty: Internet crimes including spreading enemy propaganda and disrespecting state symbols carry imprisonment; social media posts can result in prosecution
exceptions: Foreign journalists have somewhat different access arrangements under press credentials

quiz.q: What triggered Cuba's largest protests since 1994 in July 2021?
options: Electricity blackouts and food shortages combined with internet-organized mobilization
The death of a prominent dissident
quiz.explanation: Cuba's July 2021 protests were triggered by a combination of electricity blackouts, food shortages, medicine unavailability, and broader economic frustration — with social media enabling unprecedented organization, prompting the government to shut down internet access.

laws.title: Electricity Crisis and Blackouts
laws.subtitle: Grid collapse triggers unprecedented exodus wave
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's electrical grid collapsed repeatedly in 2023-2024, with blackouts lasting 20+ hours daily in some regions. The deteriorating Soviet-era infrastructure combined with fuel shortages and the US embargo created a humanitarian electricity crisis. The power outages accelerated emigration, with Cuba losing an estimated 10% of its population in a few years to migration to the US and other countries. The crisis represents the worst economic conditions since the Special Period of the 1990s.
laws.penalty: Theft of electricity infrastructure components criminally prosecuted; unauthorized power generation restricted
exceptions: Hospitals and essential services receive priority power
Government and military facilities have backup generation

quiz.q: How long did blackouts last daily in Cuba's worst-affected regions?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's grid collapse resulted in blackouts lasting 20 or more hours daily in some regions, devastating daily life and accelerating emigration.

laws.title: Mass Emigration and Population Collapse
laws.subtitle: Cuba loses unprecedented share of population in years
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has lost an estimated 10% or more of its population through emigration in just a few years, the largest exodus relative to population size in the Western Hemisphere in recent history. The combination of electrical grid collapse, food shortages, political repression and economic failure pushed over one million Cubans to leave. The US changed Cuban immigration policy repeatedly, and Cubans reached the US-Mexico border in large numbers. The demographic collapse threatens Cuba's economic recovery capacity as working-age adults leave.
laws.penalty: Cuba criminalizes unauthorized emigration attempts; people smugglers face severe criminal penalties
exceptions: Legitimate visa processes exist through lottery and family reunification
Cuba permits emigration though return can be complicated by political standing

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Cuba's population emigrated in just a few years in the early 2020s?
quiz.explanation: Cuba lost an estimated 10% or more of its population to emigration in just a few years, driven by electricity grid collapse, food shortages and political repression—the largest exodus relative to population size in recent Western Hemisphere history.

laws.title: Mobile Internet and Digital Control
laws.subtitle: Cuba grants mobile internet then uses it for surveillance
laws.fullDescription: Cuba allowed mobile internet access in 2018 for the first time, connecting millions of Cubans to the global web. The internet enabled the spread of protest organizing, with Telegram and social media coordinating the July 11, 2021 protests. The government responded with internet shutdowns during protests and increased digital surveillance. Cuba's state telecommunications company ETECSA monitors communications. The internet has simultaneously empowered Cubans and provided new surveillance tools to the government.
laws.penalty: Illegal content under Cuban law includes regime criticism on social media; ETECSA cooperates with state security for user monitoring
exceptions: Foreign journalists have different internet access arrangements
Government officials and approved entities have better connectivity

quiz.q: In what year did Cuba first allow mobile internet access to its citizens?
quiz.explanation: Cuba allowed mobile internet access in 2018 for the first time, connecting millions to the global web—though the government subsequently used internet shutdowns during protests like the July 11, 2021 demonstrations and expanded digital surveillance.

laws.title: Tourism Recovery Blocked by Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cuba's visitor numbers collapse as infrastructure fails
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's tourism industry, once a primary hard currency earner, collapsed due to the electricity crisis, hotel closures from power outages and general deterioration of infrastructure. Tourist arrivals fell dramatically from pre-COVID levels. Hotels—many operated in joint ventures with foreign companies—suffered from inability to maintain facilities without reliable electricity and supplies. The US embargo remained the primary structural constraint. Canada and Europe had been Cuba's main tourist markets but travelers increasingly chose other Caribbean destinations with reliable power.
laws.penalty: Tourism industry operates under joint venture restrictions with Cuban state; foreign currency earnings managed by state
exceptions: Private casa particular (homestay) accommodations have grown as state hotel alternative
Paladares (private restaurants) operate under expanded license framework

quiz.q: What primarily caused Cuba's tourism industry collapse beyond COVID-19?
options: Electricity crisis causing hotel closures and infrastructure deterioration
quiz.explanation: Cuba's electricity crisis—with blackouts lasting 20+ hours daily—caused hotel closures, infrastructure deterioration and guest experience failure that collapsed tourism beyond what COVID had already damaged, with travelers choosing other Caribbean destinations with reliable power.

laws.title: Environmental Law and Climate Tarea Vida
laws.subtitle: Island Nation on the Climate Frontline
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 1997 Environmental Law (Law 81) and the 2017 'Tarea Vida' (Life Task) state program address the country's extreme vulnerability to climate change. Cuba faces sea level rise threatening coastal communities, intensifying hurricanes, saltwater intrusion into agricultural land, and drought. Tarea Vida includes plans to relocate communities from flood-prone areas and restore coastal ecosystems like mangroves. Cuba's 2019 Constitution elevated environmental rights to constitutional status. Despite economic constraints, Cuba has maintained extensive forest cover and marine protected areas.
laws.penalty: Administrative fines; criminal liability for serious environmental damage; project suspension
exceptions: Essential agricultural activities
Small-scale fishing by cooperatives

laws.title: Cuba's Universal Healthcare Model
laws.subtitle: Doctors for the World
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's socialist healthcare system provides universal free healthcare to all citizens, funded by the state. Cuba's 'family doctor' program places physicians in neighborhoods, emphasizing prevention. Cuba has achieved health outcomes comparable to the US despite a fraction of GDP spending: infant mortality, life expectancy, and doctor-to-patient ratios match or exceed those of wealthy countries. Cuba trains doctors from over 100 countries at its Latin American Medical School (ELAM) and deploys medical missions internationally. Cuba also developed its own COVID-19 vaccines (Soberana, Abdala) — becoming one of the few developing nations to do so.
laws.penalty: Healthcare is free and universal; non-provision of care is a system failure, not punishable under the patient rights framework
exceptions: Top Communist Party officials have access to elite facilities
Foreign medical tourism in joint-venture hospitals

laws.title: Cuba Labor Code and State Employment
laws.subtitle: Revolutionary Workers in a Changing Economy
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Labor Code governs employment in a largely state-controlled economy. Most Cubans work for the state, which sets wages and working conditions. Cuba has expanded self-employment (cuentapropistas) and private sector work significantly since 2010, with 600,000+ self-employed workers by 2020, and legalized private companies (MIPYMES) in 2021. The minimum wage is set by the state in Cuban pesos. Cuba has strong job security — arbitrary dismissal is rare — and extensive workplace protections, but wages are very low. The labor code for self-employed and private sector workers is evolving.
laws.penalty: State employer disciplinary system; labor inspection enforces standards; criminal liability for labor law violations
exceptions: Foreign joint ventures operate under negotiated labor frameworks
Self-employed under evolving regulatory framework

laws.title: Cuba Universal Free Education
laws.subtitle: 100% Literacy in Latin America's Education Model
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 1961 Literacy Campaign — deploying 300,000 volunteers to eliminate illiteracy in one year — is a landmark achievement. Cuba provides free universal education from preschool through university, including professional medical and engineering degrees. Cuba's education quality is strong for primary and secondary — PISA-comparable assessments show Cuban students above the Latin American average. Cuba trains professionals from developing countries through the Latin American School of Medicine (ELAM). However, ideological content permeates the curriculum, and academic freedom is restricted. Access to internet and global information remains limited.
laws.penalty: Education is mandatory to age 16; school attendance laws enforced; private tutoring heavily regulated
exceptions: Religious education through Catholic and other churches has limited scope
Home schooling not recognized

laws.title: Migration Law Reform and Mass Emigration
laws.subtitle: Cuba's largest emigration wave in history
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2012 Migration Law Reform eliminated the exit permit (tarjeta blanca) that had previously required Cubans to obtain government permission to travel abroad — a major liberalization. However, Cuba's ongoing economic crisis under U.S. sanctions and inefficient state economy has driven the largest emigration wave in Cuba's history: approximately 600,000-700,000 Cubans entered the US in 2022-2023 alone, using various routes including Nicaragua (which eliminated visas for Cubans), Ecuador, and the Darién Gap. Cuba's 1966 Cuban Adjustment Act (US) gives Cubans special immigration benefits.
laws.penalty: Cubans who emigrate and engage in anti-government activities abroad may lose their property rights in Cuba; Cubans who stayed more than 24 months abroad without authorization previously lost residency (reformed in 2012); returning dissidents face arrest
exceptions: Cubans in the US benefit from the Cuban Adjustment Act and Wet-Foot/Dry-Foot policy (ended 2017)
Cuban medical professionals deployed abroad have been granted asylum in third countries
laws.sourceLabel: Cuba Migration Law Reform 2012 and Cuban Adjustment Act

quiz.q: Cuba's 2012 Migration Law Reform eliminated which requirement that had long restricted Cubans' ability to travel abroad?
options: Having a sponsor in the destination country
The exit permit (tarjeta blanca) requiring government approval to leave
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2012 reform eliminated the tarjeta blanca (white card), the exit permit Cubans had been required to obtain from the government before traveling abroad since 1961. This was a significant liberalization, though economic conditions continued to drive emigration.

laws.title: Drug Control Law
laws.subtitle: Cuba's strict drug law and special position
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Drug Control Law criminalizes drug production, trafficking, and use. Cuba has historically maintained a relatively drug-free society compared to Caribbean neighbors — attributed to strict social control, limited economic activity, and government surveillance. However, economic hardship and black market growth have increased drug use in recent years. Cannabis use has increased. Cuba has been used as a transit point for cocaine trafficking from Colombia/Venezuela. Drug trafficking can result in sentences up to 30 years or death. Cuba's healthcare-based approach treats addicts as patients.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 20-30 years to life; large-scale trafficking: death penalty; production: 15-25 years; personal use/possession: up to 3 years; drug trafficking by public officials: enhanced penalties
exceptions: Drug users may be diverted to health treatment programs
Medical narcotics available within the socialist health system
Economic necessity of small-scale dealing sometimes results in lenient sentencing
laws.sourceLabel: Cuba Ley de Control de Drogas

quiz.q: Cuba's relatively low historical drug use rates have been attributed in part to what systemic factors?
options: Strict social control, limited economic freedom, and government surveillance
quiz.explanation: Cuba's strict social control mechanisms — neighborhood surveillance committees (CDR), limited private economic activity, and government monitoring — are cited as factors that historically suppressed drug use and trafficking, though economic hardship since the Special Period has increased both.

laws.title: Same-Sex Marriage Via 2022 Referendum
laws.subtitle: Cuba legalized same-sex marriage and adoption through a public referendum in 2022
laws.fullDescription: Cuba legalized same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples through a public referendum on the Families Code in September 2022. The code passed with approximately 67% approval. This was a remarkable shift for a country that once sent gay men to forced labor camps in the 1960s under the UMAP program. Cuba's LGBTQ+ rights progress has been championed by Mariela Castro, daughter of Raúl Castro. Legal gender change is also permitted. Cuba now has one of the more progressive family law frameworks in Latin America.
laws.penalty: Discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; the Families Code provides legal equality
exceptions: Implementation and social acceptance vary across the country

quiz.q: How did Cuba legalize same-sex marriage in 2022?
options: Public referendum on the Families Code
quiz.explanation: Cuba legalized same-sex marriage through a public referendum on the new Families Code in September 2022, with approximately 67% voting in favor — a remarkable transformation for a country that once imprisoned gay men in labor camps.

laws.title: State Monopoly on Media — Independent Journalists Imprisoned
laws.subtitle: Cuba allows only state-controlled media and imprisons independent journalists
laws.fullDescription: Cuba permits only state-controlled media (Granma, Cubavision, Radio Havana Cuba). Independent journalism is illegal and treated as a crime. Following the July 2021 protests, Cuba arrested dozens of journalists and activists who documented the protests on social media. The Law 370 (Telecommunications Normalization Decree) restricts internet access and content. Internet was cut during the 2021 protests. Cuban independent journalists work clandestinely, often for international outlets. They face arrest under charges of 'subversion,' 'enemy propaganda,' and 'disorders.' Many are in prison or exile.
laws.penalty: Independent journalism treated as criminal activity; imprisonment under subversion and disorder charges; internet restricted
exceptions: State media operates under full government control

quiz.q: What did Cuba do to internet access during the 2021 protests?
quiz.explanation: Cuba cut internet access entirely during the July 2021 protests, preventing citizens and journalists from documenting or communicating about the demonstrations — a digital blackout used to suppress coverage of the largest protests Cuba had seen in decades.

laws.title: Decree 370 and Internet Shutdown During 2021 Protests
laws.subtitle: Cuba controls internet access and blocked it entirely during 2021 protests
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has one of the Caribbean's most restricted internet environments. The government controls the single internet provider (ETECSA). Decree 370 (2019) restricts online content that 'destabilizes the constitutional order' or disseminates 'counterrevolutionary' views, with fines and equipment confiscation. Mobile internet was only introduced in 2018 after decades of delay. During the July 2021 protests (the largest since 1959), Cuba shut down mobile internet entirely to prevent protest coordination and documentation. Social media platforms are accessible but monitored. Connectivity is expensive and slow. Independent digital media operates from exile.
laws.penalty: Decree 370: fines and equipment confiscation for prohibited online content; internet shutdowns during protests
exceptions: Some government and business entities have faster, less monitored connections

quiz.q: What did Cuba do to mobile internet during the historic July 2021 protests?
options: Shut it down entirely to prevent protest coordination
Limited it to 1 hour per day
quiz.explanation: During Cuba's historic July 2021 protests — the largest since 1959 — the government shut down mobile internet entirely to prevent protesters from coordinating and from sharing images of the demonstrations internationally, a digital blackout that drew international condemnation.

laws.title: BCC State Banking & Monetary Unification Crisis
laws.subtitle: Cuba eliminated its dual currency system, causing severe inflation and financial turmoil
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Banco Central de Cuba (BCC) oversees the entirely state-owned banking system. In January 2021, Cuba eliminated its dual currency system (CUC and CUP), unifying to the Cuban peso (CUP) at a heavily devalued rate — what had been 1 CUC = 25 CUP became the standard, devastating Cubans' savings denominated in the more valuable CUC. This 'tarea ordenamiento' (ordering task) triggered severe inflation exceeding 70% annually. Cuba operates under US sanctions (OFAC/CAATSA) that severely restrict banking relationships. Private individuals gained limited access to MLC (Moneda Libremente Convertible) bank accounts allowing USD-equivalent purchases at government stores. Cryptocurrency use has grown as Cubans seek alternatives.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized FX dealing: criminal prosecution; US-sanctioned Cuba-related transactions by non-Cubans: OFAC fines up to $1 million per violation; unlicensed financial operations: criminal prosecution under Cuban banking law
exceptions: Remittances from Cuban diaspora have specific regulatory channels
Humanitarian license exceptions exist for certain US transactions with Cuba
Dollar-equivalent MLC accounts are government-controlled legitimate FX mechanism

quiz.q: What was Cuba's 2021 'tarea ordenamiento' monetary reform?
options: Adopting the US dollar as legal tender
Eliminating the dual CUC/CUP currency system by converting everything to pesos
Creating a new Cuban digital currency
Joining the Latin American monetary union
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2021 'tarea ordenamiento' eliminated the dual currency system, abolishing the CUC (Cuban Convertible Peso) and unifying everything to CUP (Cuban Peso). This effectively devalued savings and triggered severe inflation.

laws.title: MINSAP & MINAG Food Safety & Cuba's Rationing Card System
laws.subtitle: Cuba's food safety exists within a state food rationing system shaped by decades of sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's food safety is managed by the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) and Ministry of Agriculture (MINAG). Cuba operates a food rationing system (libreta de abastecimiento) providing every Cuban with a monthly allocation of basic foods (rice, beans, sugar, cooking oil, eggs) at heavily subsidized prices through bodegas (state-owned stores). This system shapes how food safety works — most Cubans access state-supplied food through the rationing system, while the informal market and farmers markets (mercados agropecuarios) have different oversight. US sanctions significantly limit Cuba's access to food imports, food safety testing equipment, and food processing technology. Traditional Cuban foods — ropa vieja, black beans and rice, tostones — are prepared within this constrained system.
laws.penalty: MINSAP food safety violations: administrative sanctions; food fraud in the state distribution system: serious criminal charges; illegal food market operations outside state framework: fines and prosecution
exceptions: Private paladares (home restaurants) licensed since the 1990s have streamlined MINSAP inspection
Urban agriculture (organoponicos) has MINAG support as part of food security policy
Farmers markets (mercados agropecuarios) operate under modified state oversight

quiz.q: What is Cuba's 'libreta de abastecimiento' and how does it shape food safety considerations?
options: A certificate required to open a food business in Cuba
A food rationing booklet providing every Cuban monthly basic food allocations at subsidized prices through state stores
A tourism menu required at all Cuban restaurants serving foreigners
A food safety inspection certificate displayed by Cuban restaurants
quiz.explanation: Cuba's libreta de abastecimiento (supply booklet) is a food rationing card providing each Cuban household monthly allocations of basic foods — rice, beans, sugar, cooking oil, eggs, coffee — at heavily subsidized prices through state bodegas. The system has existed since the 1960s and shapes food distribution, food safety oversight, and food security across Cuba.

laws.title: Cuba Animal Welfare Framework — Limited Formal Protections
laws.subtitle: Cuba has basic animal protection but no comprehensive welfare law
laws.fullDescription: Cuba lacks a comprehensive national animal welfare law. Animal cruelty is addressed patchily through sanitary regulations and municipal ordinances, with no specific animal welfare statute. Cuba's agricultural system is state-controlled, making livestock welfare a state affair. Companion animal welfare is increasingly recognized culturally, with some Cuban NGOs and veterinary school networks advocating for better protections. The Cuban Veterinary Medical Association promotes humane treatment. Urban Havana has seen growing pet culture, but stray animal management remains limited and euthanasia-based. Cuba's economic constraints limit resources for animal welfare enforcement significantly.
laws.penalty: General sanctions under Código Penal for damage to property; administrative fines for violations of sanitary regulations; limited specific animal cruelty penalties
exceptions: State livestock operations
Pest control
Research under university oversight
laws.sourceLabel: Cuban Regulatory Framework (No Comprehensive Animal Welfare Law)

quiz.q: What is the primary gap in Cuba's animal welfare legal framework?
options: Cuba has no comprehensive national animal welfare law
quiz.explanation: Cuba lacks a comprehensive national animal welfare statute. Animal cruelty is addressed only patchily through sanitary regulations and municipal ordinances, with no dedicated animal welfare law — a significant gap compared to many Latin American neighbors.

laws.title: Cuba Código de las Familias 2022 — Same-Sex Marriage by Referendum
laws.subtitle: Cuba legalized same-sex marriage in a 2022 referendum
laws.fullDescription: Cuba enacted a revolutionary new Código de las Familias (Family Code) in 2022 — approved by referendum with 67% support. The code legalized same-sex marriage, same-sex adoption, and surrogacy. Cuba became the first Caribbean country to allow same-sex marriage through popular vote. The new Family Code replaced the 1975 Family Code and embraced a pluralist view of family structures including single-parent, extended, and same-sex families. Cuba's family law also significantly strengthened children's rights, including the right to be heard in family proceedings. The Code also addresses family violence comprehensively. Despite the political system's authoritarianism in other areas, Cuba's family law moved to be among Latin America's most progressive.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement through tribunales municipales and provinciales; criminal penalties under Código Penal for domestic violence; state support through INDER programs
exceptions: Pre-marital property retained
Special provisions for agricultural/cooperative families
State housing allocation rules intersect with family property division
laws.sourceLabel: Código de las Familias de Cuba (2022)

quiz.q: What historic family law milestone did Cuba achieve in 2022?
options: Cuba became the first country to ban all divorce
Cuba became the first Caribbean country to legalize same-sex marriage through popular referendum
Cuba abolished private property in family law
Cuba made marriage mandatory for all couples with children
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2022 Código de las Familias — approved by referendum — made Cuba the first Caribbean country to legalize same-sex marriage through popular vote. The new Family Code also recognized same-sex adoption and surrogacy, representing a remarkable shift for a country with a complex history on LGBTQ+ rights.

laws.title: Cuba Property Rights & 2019 Constitutional Reform
laws.subtitle: Gradual private property recognition under socialism
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2019 constitution made landmark changes to property rights, explicitly recognizing private property for the first time since the 1959 revolution (Article 22), alongside socialist state property (Art. 18) and cooperative property. Cubans were allowed to own multiple properties from 2011 under Raul Castro's reforms. The 2011 Guidelines (Lineamientos) also legalized private sale and purchase of homes and cars after decades of prohibition. However, the state retains dominant ownership of productive enterprises. Cubans can sell private homes but the market remains limited by low purchasing power and emigration.
laws.penalty: Expropriation for public benefit with compensation; state retains right to nationalize for social interest
exceptions: Multiple property ownership allowed since 2011
Private businesses expanded under 2021 MIPYMES regulations
laws.source: Constitucion de la Republica Art. 18-22 (2019); Lineamientos 2011

quiz.q: What significant change did Cuba's 2019 constitution make regarding private property?
options: It explicitly recognized private property for the first time since 1959
It transferred all homes to state ownership
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2019 constitution explicitly recognized private property (Article 22) for the first time since the 1959 revolution, a landmark change acknowledging the reforms allowing private home sales and small businesses since 2011.

laws.title: Cuba Consumer Rights & Dual Economy
laws.subtitle: Socialist consumer protections in a dual-currency economy
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's consumer protection operates within a socialist framework where the state controls most production and distribution. The Office for Protection of Economic Rights of Citizens (ODPE) handles consumer complaints, primarily about state enterprises. The 2021 unification of the Cuban peso (elimination of the CUC dual currency) created significant inflation and consumer hardship. Private sector expansion under the MIPYMES regulations (2021) created a new private consumer market. The state-run RECLAMACIONES system handles product defect claims against state enterprises. Informal market practices are widespread given chronic shortages. Online purchasing is very limited due to internet restrictions and international sanctions.
laws.penalty: State enterprise defect: replacement or credit with RECLAMACIONES; private MIPYME violation: administrative fine
exceptions: 2021 currency unification caused major inflation affecting consumer purchasing power
Private MIPYMES now subject to consumer protection rules
laws.source: Constitucion Art. 77; ODPE Regulations; MIPYMES Decree-Laws 2021

quiz.q: What major economic change in Cuba in 2021 significantly impacted consumer purchasing power?
options: The introduction of Bitcoin as legal tender
The elimination of the dual-currency (CUC) system causing significant inflation
A trade deal with the United States
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2021 monetary unification (Tarea Ordenamiento) eliminated the dual-currency system (Cuban Peso and CUC), unifying to a single peso at a rate that effectively devalued state workers' salaries by up to 75%, causing significant inflation and reduced consumer purchasing power.

laws.title: Constitución de Cuba 2019 — One-Party State
laws.subtitle: 2019 constitution — socialist state with PCC monopoly
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2019 Constitution replaced the 1976 Marxist-Leninist constitution while maintaining the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) as the 'leading force of society and the state.' The 2019 constitution recognized private property more broadly, introduced market concepts, and allowed same-sex civil unions (later approved by referendum in 2022). The President is now separate from the head of government (Prime Minister). The National Assembly elects the President. Cuba holds elections — but only PCC-approved candidates may run for most offices. 2021 protest law (Decree-Law 35) criminalized online dissent.
laws.penalty: 'Crimes against the state': 3-20 years. Anti-revolutionary activities: 4-10 years. Online dissent (Decree-Law 35): up to 15 years.
exceptions: Municipal delegate elections allow multiple candidates (though PCC pre-screened)
Citizens may propose 'popular initiatives' to the National Assembly
Religious practice permitted within patriotic framework

quiz.q: Which political party does Cuba's 2019 Constitution designate as the 'leading force of society and the state'?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2019 Constitution explicitly designates the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) as the 'leading force of society and the state' — embedding one-party rule in the constitutional text. While the constitution recognizes broader economic rights, the PCC maintains political monopoly.

laws.title: Embargo Estadounidense — US Embargo on Cuba
laws.subtitle: Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act 1996 (Helms-Burton)
laws.fullDescription: The US embargo on Cuba (known in Cuba as 'el bloqueo' — the blockade) began in 1962 under President Kennedy, following the expropriation of US properties. The 1996 Helms-Burton Act (Libertad Act) codified the embargo into law, requiring Congressional approval to lift it. Title III allows US nationals to sue foreign companies that 'traffic' in confiscated US property — activated by Trump in 2019. Cuba argues the embargo causes $4+ billion in annual damages. The Obama administration's 2014-2016 partial rapprochement was reversed by Trump. The embargo remains US policy.
laws.penalty: US persons violating Cuba embargo: civil fines up to $1 million, criminal prosecution. Third-country companies face US secondary sanctions.
exceptions: Food and medicine have been partially exempted since 2000
Academic and cultural exchanges allowed under specific licenses
Cuban-Americans may send remittances within regulatory limits

quiz.q: Which US law, passed in 1996, codified the Cuba embargo and required Congressional approval to lift it?
quiz.explanation: The Helms-Burton Act (Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act, 1996) codified the Cuba embargo into law — previously it was executive policy that a president could change. Helms-Burton also introduced Title III allowing US nationals to sue foreign companies using expropriated US properties, which Trump activated in 2019.

laws.title: Sistema de Salud Cubano — Universal Healthcare
laws.subtitle: Cuba's health system — high outcomes despite poverty
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has universal free healthcare with outcomes comparable to developed countries: life expectancy 78+ years, infant mortality ~4/1,000 (similar to US). The system is community-based with family doctor-and-nurse teams (médico de la familia) in every neighborhood. Cuba trains more doctors per capita than any country and exports healthcare workers globally (generating $11+ billion in revenue — Cuba's largest export). Despite high quality by outcome metrics, the system suffers chronic medicine shortages due to the US embargo and economic mismanagement. Cuba's COVID-19 vaccines (Soberana, Abdala) were produced domestically.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for patients. Medical negligence: civil liability, professional license review.
exceptions: Health tourism sector serves foreign patients at market prices separately
Military health services slightly differentiated
US embargo creates formal barriers to some medical equipment procurement

quiz.q: What is Cuba's largest export by revenue?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's largest export by revenue is healthcare workers — specifically medical missions that provide doctors, nurses, and health professionals to countries in Latin America, Africa, and elsewhere. These medical missions generate over $11 billion annually, far exceeding Cuba's sugar, nickel, tobacco, or rum exports.

laws.title: Artículo 68 — Dissent and Political Prisoners
laws.subtitle: Criminal penalties for political opposition in Cuba
laws.fullDescription: Cuba imprisons political dissidents, journalists, and activists through various criminal statutes. After the July 11, 2021 (11-J) protests — Cuba's largest civil unrest since 1994 — over 1,000 protesters were arrested, with hundreds sentenced to 5-25 years for 'sedition,' 'disorder,' and 'contempt.' Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the UN have documented Cuba's political prisoners. The UNPACU, MDL, and other opposition groups operate underground. Cuba's legal system allows trials without defense lawyers for national security cases. Freedom of the press is constitutionally subordinated to 'social purposes.'
laws.penalty: Sedition: up to 30 years. Contempt (desacato): 1-5 years. 'Enemy propaganda': 1-8 years.
exceptions: Prisoners transferred to house arrest may be released after diplomatic pressure
Some political prisoners released in exchanges with other countries
Religious activities increasingly tolerated

quiz.q: Approximately how many people were arrested following Cuba's July 11, 2021 protests?
quiz.explanation: Over 1,000 people were arrested following Cuba's July 11, 2021 protests — the largest civil demonstrations since 1994. Hundreds received prison sentences of 5-25 years for charges including sedition, disorder, and contempt. International human rights organizations documented the mass prosecutions as politically motivated.

laws.title: Libreta de Abastecimiento — Rationing Book
laws.subtitle: Cuba's rationing system since 1962
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's libreta de abastecimiento (supply booklet) has rationed basic goods since 1962. Cuban families receive monthly subsidized rations of rice, beans, cooking oil, sugar, salt, eggs, and some other items through state bodegas. The ration provides only a fraction of monthly nutritional needs — additional food must be purchased from state stores (in CUP) or the informal market (in USD/MLC). The dual-currency system (CUP and MLC/USD) created a two-tier economy. The 2021 monetary unification eliminated the CUC, but USD is increasingly needed for quality goods.
laws.penalty: Rationing fraud: criminal prosecution. Black market trading: administrative fines and confiscation.
exceptions: Diabetics, children, and elderly receive modified ration allocations
Special rations for pregnant women and infants
Workers in certain sectors receive additional food benefits

quiz.q: Cuba's rationing system (libreta) has been in operation since what year?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's rationing system (libreta de abastecimiento) was introduced in 1962 following US trade restrictions and the nationalization of industries. The libreta provides subsidized basic goods to all Cuban households, though it typically covers only a fraction of monthly food needs.

laws.title: Emigración — Cuban Migration Rights
laws.subtitle: Migration reform 2013 — travel and emigration rights
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2013 migration reform eliminated the 'White Card' (tarjeta blanca) requirement that Cubans needed government permission to travel abroad. Cubans may now travel freely for up to 24 months before losing residency rights. The Cuban Adjustment Act (US law, 1966) allowed Cubans who reached US soil to adjust to permanent residency. The 2023 migration crisis saw record Cubans migrating — over 300,000 encountered at the US border in 2023. Migration to the US often occurs through Nicaragua (visa-free entry) to Mexico and then the US border. 'Dry foot/wet foot' policy ended in 2017.
laws.penalty: Professionals (doctors) who abandon government medical missions abroad face career sanctions and restricted return.
exceptions: Cuban Adjustment Act (US law) provides preferential immigration status for Cubans in the US
Humanitarian parole program for Cubans to US expanded 2023
Cubans in third countries may apply for US immigrant visas normally

quiz.q: In what year did Cuba eliminate the 'White Card' requirement for Cubans to travel abroad?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2013 migration reform eliminated the tarjeta blanca (White Card) — the government permission slip previously required for Cubans to travel or emigrate. After the reform, Cubans could travel on a regular passport for up to 24 months before losing residency rights.

laws.title: Moneda Nacional — Currency Unification 2021
laws.subtitle: CUC eliminated — peso/MLC dual system remains
laws.fullDescription: Cuba operated a dual currency system for decades: the Cuban Peso (CUP) for domestic transactions and the Convertible Peso (CUC) at parity with the USD. In January 2021, Cuba unified the currency, eliminating the CUC. The official rate was set at 24 CUP = 1 USD. However, a parallel USD-denominated MLC (Moneda Libremente Convertible) system for foreign currency was maintained. Inflation surged after unification — reaching 70%+ in 2021. State salaries increased in CUP but purchasing power fell due to inflation. The informal USD rate diverged significantly from the official 24 CUP rate.
laws.penalty: Black market currency exchange: criminal prosecution, confiscation of currency.
exceptions: Remittances from abroad may be received in MLC cards
Tourist facilities operate in MLC/USD
Some state enterprises have USD income streams

quiz.q: What was Cuba's official exchange rate set at during the 2021 currency unification?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2021 currency unification set the official rate at 24 Cuban Pesos (CUP) = 1 US Dollar, replacing the old dual system where the CUC was at 1:1 parity with USD. However, the informal market exchange rate quickly diverged to 80-120+ CUP per dollar, reflecting actual purchasing power.

laws.title: Educación Gratuita — Free Education System
laws.subtitle: Universal free education from preschool to university
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's constitutional right to free education covers all levels from preschool through university and postgraduate. Literacy campaigns (1961 literacy campaign, Operation Alpha, reduced illiteracy from 23% to under 4%) are celebrated globally. Cuba's adult literacy rate is 99.7%. The Escuelas al Campo program historically required students to work in agriculture. Cuban universities produce large numbers of graduates especially in medicine, engineering, and sciences. The Cuban government uses education internationally as soft power through scholarship programs.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for students. Academic dishonesty: expulsion, grade invalidation. Unauthorized private tutoring: administrative fines.
exceptions: Religious private schools closed in 1961 — all education is public
Foreign students may enroll in Cuban universities under government programs
Some technical vocational programs have modified content

quiz.q: What was Cuba's pre-revolution adult literacy rate before the 1961 literacy campaign?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's literacy rate was approximately 77% before the 1961 literacy campaign, meaning about 23% of adults were illiterate. The campaign — sending 100,000 volunteers throughout the country — reduced illiteracy to under 4% within a year, widely regarded as one of the most successful literacy campaigns in history.

laws.title: Política Ambiental — Cuba's Environmental Framework
laws.subtitle: Law 81 (1997) — environmental protection in socialist context
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's environmental law (Law 81, 1997) established CITMA (Ministry of Science, Technology, and Environment) as the primary environmental authority. Cuba has a relatively good environmental record compared to GDP — low car ownership, organic farming out of necessity, and limited industrialization. Cuba converted much of its agriculture to organic/low-input methods after the 'Special Period' (Soviet collapse, 1989-1993). The UN Development Programme praised Cuba's human development/ecological footprint balance. However, Havana Bay and river pollution remain challenges. Cuba has 100+ protected natural areas.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations: CITMA fines, activity suspension, criminal prosecution for serious damage.
exceptions: Small subsistence farming activities have simplified environmental requirements
Scientific research with CITMA permits in protected areas
Emergency economic activities may receive temporary exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: CITMA — Ministerio de Ciencia, Tecnología y Medio Ambiente

quiz.q: What forced Cuba to convert much of its agriculture to organic methods?
options: The Special Period following Soviet collapse (1989-1993)
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 'Special Period' following the Soviet Union's collapse (1989-1993) eliminated access to chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and petroleum-based inputs that Cuba had imported from the USSR. Out of necessity, Cuba converted much of its agriculture to organic and low-input methods, inadvertently creating one of the world's most extensive organic farming systems.

laws.title: Código de Familia 2022 — Family Law Reform
laws.subtitle: Same-sex marriage and diverse families legalized by referendum
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's 2022 Family Code (approved by referendum in September 2022 with 66.9% approval) legalized same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples, polyamorous family recognition, children's rights to participation in family decisions, elderly rights, and expanded protections for domestic workers. Cuba became the first Caribbean country to constitutionally recognize same-sex marriage. The code replaced the 1975 Family Code. Despite the progressive family law, Cuba simultaneously imprisoned LGBTQ+ rights activists who sought to organize independently from PCC-approved structures.
laws.penalty: Family code violations (child abuse, domestic violence): criminal prosecution. Marriage fraud: civil nullification.
exceptions: Religious institutions may decline to perform same-sex ceremonies
Traditional family structures remain recognized
Inheritance and property rights follow family code provisions

quiz.q: What percentage of Cubans voted to approve the 2022 Family Code by referendum?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2022 Family Code was approved by 66.9% of voters in a September 2022 referendum. The code legalized same-sex marriage and adoption, making Cuba the first Caribbean country to constitutionally recognize same-sex marriage — though human rights groups noted the simultaneous imprisonment of independent LGBTQ+ activists.

laws.title: Empresas Mixtas — Joint Ventures in Cuba
laws.subtitle: Foreign investment law — joint ventures with Cuban state
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Foreign Investment Law (Law 118, 2014) regulates foreign investment through joint ventures — typically requiring the Cuban state to have a stake. Wholly foreign-owned companies are allowed in limited sectors. Cuba has attracted investment in tourism, mining, telecommunications, and energy. Key investors include Spanish (Meliá Hotels), Chinese (telecom), and Canadian (mining) companies. The Mariel Special Development Zone offers enhanced incentives. Foreign investments require Council of Ministers approval. Employee hiring must go through a state employment agency (eliminating direct employer-employee relationships).
laws.penalty: Violations of joint venture agreements: contract arbitration (Cuban International Commercial Arbitration Court). Unauthorized foreign investment: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Mariel Special Development Zone has 100% foreign ownership in some sectors
Cooperative investment models without full joint venture have emerged
Some humanitarian investments (food, medicine) have simplified approval

quiz.q: What unusual employment requirement do foreign companies in Cuba face?
options: Must hire employees through a state employment agency
Must train Cuban replacements within 5 years
quiz.explanation: Foreign companies investing in Cuba must hire employees through a Cuban state employment agency (typically Cubalse or sector-specific agencies) rather than directly employing workers. The state agency pays workers in CUP, while companies pay the agency in hard currency — a major source of state revenue and a mechanism for controlling worker-employer relationships.

laws.title: Crisis Energética — Electricity Blackouts
laws.subtitle: Cuba's energy crisis — 10+ hour daily blackouts
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has experienced severe electricity blackouts since 2019, worsening dramatically in 2022-2024. The electricity grid, based on aging Soviet-era thermoelectric plants and insufficient fuel imports (due to the embargo and economic crisis), cannot meet demand. Blackouts of 10-20 hours per day have become routine in some provinces. The government has contracted floating power plants and received Russian and Venezuelan fuel assistance. The energy crisis is a major driver of emigration. Photovoltaic solar panels are increasingly imported but distributed unevenly.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized electricity connections or tampering with meters: criminal prosecution. Industrial electricity theft: civil and criminal liability.
exceptions: Hospitals and emergency services have priority grid access
Hotels serving foreign tourists have backup generation
Government buildings have backup power systems

quiz.q: What has been a major driver of Cuba's 2022-2024 mass emigration?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's severe electricity crisis — with blackouts of 10-20 hours per day in 2022-2024, combined with food shortages, medicine unavailability, and economic collapse — became a major driver of mass emigration. Cuba saw record emigration levels, with over 300,000 Cubans encountered at the US border in 2023.

laws.title: Decreto-Ley 370 — Internet Censorship
laws.subtitle: Social media control — 'information contrary to social interest'
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's Decree-Law 370 (2019) regulates internet use and prohibits online content deemed to be against 'constitutional order, morality, and decorum.' Decree-Law 35 (2021) criminalized 'cyber-terrorism' and content causing 'social alarm' — used against protesters and journalists. Cuba has significantly expanded internet access (from near-zero in 2018 to 60%+ mobile internet penetration by 2022) but simultaneously increased digital repression. Activists use VPNs (technically illegal). Twitter, Facebook, WhatsApp are used when internet is available but subject to throttling during protests.
laws.penalty: Online 'destabilization': up to 15 years (Decree-Law 35). 'Information contrary to social interest': fines up to 3,000 CUP.
exceptions: Academic and professional internet use has some protection
Government-approved online commerce platforms operate freely
Foreign journalists may access internet more freely (in theory)

quiz.q: What Cuban law passed in 2021 criminalized online 'cyber-terrorism' and content causing 'social alarm'?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Decree-Law 35 (2021) criminalized 'cyber-terrorism' and online content that causes 'social alarm' or undermines 'constitutional order.' It was passed shortly after the July 11, 2021 protests, which were coordinated via social media. Dozens of activists and journalists were prosecuted under Decree-Law 35.

laws.title: Cuentapropismo — Self-Employment Expansion
laws.subtitle: 2021 expansion to 2,000+ private business activities
laws.fullDescription: Cuba expanded private self-employment (cuentapropismo) dramatically in 2021, expanding the list of authorized private activities from 127 to 2,000+, and creating the MIPYME (micro, small, and medium enterprise) legal category. Private restaurants (paladares), taxis, homestays (casas particulares), and retail have grown significantly. By 2023, over 10,000 small businesses were registered. However, private businesses face import restrictions, USD access problems, and supply chain challenges. The expansion followed post-1990 reforms but represents the most significant private sector opening since the revolution.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed self-employment: fines, goods confiscation, criminal prosecution. Tax evasion from private business: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Cultural and artistic activities have broader self-employment permissions
Agricultural cooperatives (CPA, CCS, UBPC) have separate frameworks
Diplomatic household workers operate under special permits
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Trabajo y Seguridad Social — Cuba

quiz.q: How many private business activities did Cuba authorize after its 2021 MIPYME reform?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2021 MIPYME reform expanded the list of authorized private self-employment activities from 127 to over 2,000. This represented a major shift — for the first time, everything not explicitly prohibited was permitted (rather than only the explicit list). By 2023, over 10,000 small businesses were registered.

laws.title: Turismo — Tourism as Key Industry
laws.subtitle: Tourism generates $2-3B — central to Cuba's hard currency
laws.fullDescription: Tourism is Cuba's primary hard currency earner, with 4+ million visitors annually pre-COVID (2019). The industry is state-controlled through GAVIOTA (military-run), Cubanacán, and MINTUR. Cuba's tourism model features all-inclusive beach resorts (Varadero, Cayo Coco, Cayo Santa María) largely separate from local communities ('tourist apartheid' criticism). The 2020-2022 COVID crisis devastated tourism. US citizens cannot travel to Cuba for tourism (embargo) but may visit under licensed categories (educational, journalistic, etc.). Canada and Europe provide most tourists.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed tourist operations (private): fines, closure. Association with foreign tourists by ordinary Cubans in unauthorized contexts: administrative interventions.
exceptions: Licensed casas particulares (B&Bs) may legally host foreign tourists
Paladares (private restaurants) serve tourists under license
Authorized cultural and educational programs allow broader contact

quiz.q: Which organization controls most of Cuba's tourism industry?
options: GAVIOTA (military-run tourism group) and state companies
quiz.explanation: Cuba's tourism industry is dominated by GAVIOTA (a military-run tourism conglomerate), Cubanacán, and Gran Caribe — all state entities. GAVIOTA alone controls over 50% of Cuba's hotel rooms. The military's commercial role through GAVIOTA has been criticized by US human rights advocates.

laws.title: Tribunal Supremo Popular — Judicial System
laws.subtitle: Cuba's people's courts — no judicial independence
laws.fullDescription: Cuba's judicial system operates under the principle of 'popular justice' with lay judges (escabinos) alongside professional judges. The Supreme People's Court is elected by the National Assembly and accounts to it — not independent. Criminal cases involving national security may be tried by military tribunals. Defense lawyers are members of ONBC (National Organization of Collective Law Offices) — a state body. Cuba's criminal procedure (Law 5/1977) allows extended pretrial detention. Cuba has no jury system for most crimes. The Bar Association is state-controlled.
laws.penalty: Crimes against state order: judicial proceedings without true adversarial defense. Pretrial detention can be extended indefinitely for national security cases.
exceptions: Some cases have appeal procedures to higher chambers
Foreigners may have consular notification rights
Child justice handled by separate family courts

quiz.q: To what body is Cuba's Supreme People's Court accountable?
options: The Cuban people through annual elections
quiz.explanation: Cuba's Supreme People's Court is elected by and accountable to the National Assembly — not an independent judicial body. This contrasts with democratic systems where courts are independent of the legislature. Cuba's constitution does not include judicial independence as a principle.

laws.title: Industria Azucarera — Sugar Industry Decline
laws.subtitle: From world's top producer to severely reduced output
laws.fullDescription: Cuba was once the world's largest sugar exporter — sugar dominated the economy for 150 years. At its peak (1970 — the 'Zafra de los Diez Millones'), Cuba attempted to produce 10 million tons. The Soviet collapse (1989) eliminated subsidized markets. Sugar production collapsed from 7-8 million tons in the 1970s to under 1 million tons by 2022. AZCUBA (state sugar company) manages the remaining industry. Sugar land has been converted to other crops (rice, vegetables, cattle) or lies idle. The sugarcane-based rum industry (Havana Club) remains a significant export.
laws.penalty: Sugar quota violations: AZCUBA administrative proceedings. Illegal sale of sugar: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Artisanal rum and guarapo (cane juice) production by cooperatives
Export under government contracts exempt from domestic price controls
Sugar for domestic rationing priced differently from export

quiz.q: What was Cuba's sugar production target in the famous 1970 'Zafra de los Diez Millones'?
quiz.explanation: The 1970 'Zafra de los Diez Millones' (Ten Million Ton Harvest) was Cuba's attempt to produce 10 million tons of sugar — a massive national mobilization. Cuba fell short (producing 8.5 million tons — still a record) and the effort severely disrupted the rest of the economy. The campaign is a cautionary tale in Cuban economic history.

laws.title: Vivienda — Housing Crisis in Cuba
laws.subtitle: Severe housing shortage — 862,000 unit deficit
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has a severe housing shortage — an estimated 862,000 unit deficit. The housing stock is deteriorating: many colonial-era buildings in Havana collapse annually. Cubans cannot easily buy or sell homes (until 2011 reforms limited to one primary and one vacation home). Housing construction has been minimal due to lack of materials and financing. The 2011 reform allowing real estate sales created a market, but prices quickly dollarized beyond ordinary Cubans' reach. After the 2022 earthquakes in Santiago and 2017 Hurricane Irma, housing reconstruction remains incomplete.
laws.penalty: Illegal squatting in abandoned property: eviction, possible criminal trespass. Unauthorized real estate transactions: confiscation, fines.
exceptions: Interpersonal permuta (house swaps) are the traditional housing exchange mechanism
Government provides emergency housing after natural disasters
Cuban diaspora remittances increasingly fund housing improvements
laws.sourceLabel: Instituto Nacional de la Vivienda — Cuba

quiz.q: Cuba's 2011 housing reform allowed citizens to do what for the first time in decades?
options: Build their own homes without permits
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2011 housing reform allowed Cubans to legally buy and sell real estate for the first time since the revolution. Previously, homes could only be transferred through permuta (house swaps) or inheritance. The reform created a real estate market, though prices quickly dollarized beyond many Cubans' purchasing power.

laws.title: Bahía de La Habana — Bay Cleanup Program
laws.subtitle: Havana Bay remediation — industrial pollution
laws.fullDescription: Havana Bay became severely polluted from industrial discharge, sewage, and fuel spills during the Soviet era. A major remediation program (1990s-present) has removed industrial facilities, improved sewage treatment, and partially restored water quality. Fish have returned to the bay. The program has been a rare environmental success story in Cuba. However, the southern part of the bay still receives significant sewage. Climate change threatens Havana's low-lying areas — saltwater intrusion and flooding are growing concerns. Cuba has adopted a National Climate Change Plan ('Tarea Vida') for coastal adaptation.
laws.penalty: Industrial discharge into Havana Bay: CITMA administrative sanctions, civil damages. Sewage violations by state facilities: government administrative proceedings.
exceptions: Legacy pollutants (historical contamination) have specialized remediation funding
Emergency fuel spills from Russian tankers handled under bilateral agreements
Small fishing boats have modified environmental requirements

quiz.q: What is the name of Cuba's national climate change adaptation plan?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's national climate change adaptation plan is called 'Tarea Vida' (Life Task), adopted in 2017. It focuses on coastal protection, agriculture adaptation, water management, and resilience building for Cuba's most vulnerable areas. Cuba is particularly vulnerable to sea-level rise, hurricanes, and drought.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Rights — CENESEX and Tensions
laws.subtitle: State-sponsored LGBTQ+ activism vs. independent voices
laws.fullDescription: Cuba has a contradictory LGBTQ+ record. CENESEX (National Center for Sex Education), led by Mariela Castro (Raúl's daughter), has promoted state-endorsed LGBTQ+ rights — including the 2022 Family Code legalizing same-sex marriage. However, independent LGBTQ+ activists who seek to organize outside the PCC framework are repressed. The 2019 'conga' (LGBTQ+ pride march not authorized by CENESEX) was violently dispersed and organizers arrested. Cuba decriminalized homosexuality in 1979 but had previously (1960s) sent gay men to 'rehabilitation camps' (UMAP). Trans healthcare is available through the public system.
laws.penalty: 'Counterrevolutionary' LGBTQ+ organizing: arrest, prosecution under broad political crime statutes.
exceptions: CENESEX-affiliated activities are legal and promoted
State hospitals provide trans medical procedures
Same-sex families have full legal rights under the 2022 Family Code
laws.sourceLabel: CENESEX — Centro Nacional de Educación Sexual

quiz.q: Cuba's 2022 Family Code was approved by what mechanism?
quiz.explanation: Cuba's 2022 Family Code was approved by a popular referendum on September 25, 2022, with 66.9% voting in favor. This made Cuba the first Caribbean country to constitutionally recognize same-sex marriage through a direct democratic vote, despite Cuba not being a full democracy by international standards.
